speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the great honour to present a petition from dozens and dozens of people in my constituency. They are calling upon Parliament to do whatever is necessary to resolve the plight of refugees currently in Canada and make decisions humanely and promptly to allow these individuals to plan their lives.
The petitioners' particular concern is for those people who have been separated from their families for many, many years. They want the situation to be redressed as quickly as possible.
I have a further petition from residents of Toronto, East York, Don Mills, Victoria Village, all raising the concern related to the separation of spouses as a result of the refugee and immigration processes.
The petitioners are calling upon Parliament to do whatever is necessary to allow families to be reunited within a reasonable amount of time, i.e. no longer than one year.
We all know the plight of families of immigrants and refugees who are separated from one another. Obviously this is a situation that has to be redressed quickly.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition from several dozen
farmers from southwestern Ontario deploring the lack of government support.
Last year government support programs were cut by 40 per cent at a time when the world price for grain was dropping by almost a similar amount.
The petitioners are calling on government to provide the same assistance that would have been provided had the new safety net system been in effect during the 1990-91 crop year.
In fact, when the government finally made an announcement, it was only for about half the amount that was needed. The minister is supposed to be making an announcement at eleven o'clock this morning spelling out the exact details of that arrangement.
In any event it is clear to these producers that in fact the government has short-changed them by almost 50 per cent, and the payment is over a year late.

The House resumed from Friday, November 8, consideration of the motion of Ms. Campbell (Vancouver Centre) that Bill C-12, an act to amend the Young Offenders Act and the Criminal Code, be read the third time and passed.

November 21, 1991
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, the goal of a safe, law abiding society is one we all pursue and we in this Chamber feel a particular responsibility to work toward.
We have all been shocked by the information on the escalation of youth crime. All Canadians want to get the problem under control. We in the Liberal Party believe this legislation is taking the wrong direction to ensure a society that is safer both in the short term and in the long term.
The goal of the Young Offenders Act when it was passed nearly a decade ago was to protect society in two ways. In the short term the purpose was to ensure that youth convicted of crimes dangerous to society were in secure detention when that was necessary. But the second goal was to ensure that every possible step was taken to protect society from a life-long criminal, in other words to ensure that the young offender did not become a life-long threat to public safety and security.
The belief was that youth detention centres should provide not only incarceration for the immediate protection of society, but rehabilitation, counselling and training that would allow a young offender at a crossroad in life to change from a damaged young person into a contributing, fulfilled member of society.
The purpose was also to separate the young offenders from hardened criminals so that they would not be detained in a place where they would veiy quickly and effectively learn the patterns of crime for a lifetime and all the skills of crime.
For over 16 months this bill has been before committee. There have been numerous witnesses from all parts of the justice system and the system dealing with youth. The bill has been universally criticized for the direction it takes. It has been called regressive and mired in outdated premises and concepts.
The bill is not based on the notion that society has failed if a child ends up in prison. Rather than deal with the reality of the causes of youth crime and how best to rehabilitate young offenders and avoid a life-long problem for society, the bill in fact makes it easier to penalize children in the adult criminal system and to abandon them forever to a life of hardened crime.
After nine years we know there are problems with the legislation and with the system that implements the
legislation and that changes are needed. A big failing is that the needed facilities for the detention and treatment of young offenders have not materialized. The courts, knowing this, are not necessarily mandating detention when they should. The necessary support services have not been provided in communities for young offenders so that the appropriate level of supervision can be provided while a young offender is reintegrated into society at a pace that maximizes at least the potential that the young offender will return to the community as a healthy, adjusted, productive citizen.
Because the resources have not been provided, one thing that is happening is the privatization of detention and treatment services. It is one thing to privatize a baseball stadium, but it is quite another thing to leave to the private sector the treatment of damaged and vulnerable young people.
One benefit of privatizing the system is deemed to be cheaper provision of services. The reason it may be cheaper is that outside the public system it is easier to pay low salaries. The result of that is a rapid turnover of personnel in detention facilities so that those who are dealing with young people are constantly new on the job and inexperienced.
In the privatized facilities there is inadequate control of the delivery of programs, particularly of the rehabilitation programs that the centres are intended to provide. There is inadequate provision for the reintegration of the released young offender into society. There is little control over the fact that there may be very vulnerable 12-year-olds in with reasonably hardened 18-year old young offenders.
This bill does not deal with these issues. It fails to deal totally with the need for a comprehensive rehabilitative program which we and most witnesses heard on this bill have recommended. Instead the solution the government proposes is to transfer the young offender to the adult justice system, to the adult court, and eventually to the adult prison where the school for crime in the life of this young person can come fully into operation.
This bill is giving up on these young people and on the whole intention of the Young Offenders Act. We are trying to avoid for the young offender and for society someone who is constantly in society as a cost and as a risk.
November 21, 1991

Another compelling reason why this is the wrong answer is the unequal treatment that young offenders receive across Canada. In one province, for instance, the chance of the young offender being transferred to criminal court is as little as 15 per cent, whereas it is as great as 87 per cent in another province. The federal government has to take responsibility for the fact that there is no consistency in treatment of young offenders across Canada. Surely, if we have a nation, it is because we believe there are certain national standards for national programs and national rights that exist within Canada, wherever one happens to live.
A second reason for condemning this approach is the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. It requires that young offenders be incarcerated separately from adult offenders. It is not good enough to have a lot of press conferences around an international conference on the child and then ignore the international obligations to our children.
Just two weeks ago in Canada we had a national symposium on children and youth; 400 people from across Canada were here when that symposium ended to meet with parliamentarians and make us aware of the crisis facing our young people. They described some situations to us and asked for our urgent action. They are directly relevant to the bill before us today and to the fact that we do have a high rate of young offenders and we are not dealing with them adequately.
Poverty is one of the underlying reasons for the escalation in youth crime. We may all know the figures but I think they need to be repeated again and again and again, until we understand that they are a tragedy in one of the wealthiest countries of the world and they need to be dealt with. One million children live in poverty in Canada. The largest single group of poor in Canadian society is our children. One out of every six children we meet on the street is poor. In 1989 there were 62,000 more poor children in Canada. The problem is getting worse and not better. At many food banks 40 per cent of those being helped are children.
Right here in Ottawa, within the shadow of this building, one child in four lives in a family whose income is insufficient for basic necessities. Some neighbourhoods close to Parliament Hill have a child poverty rate in excess of 35 per cent. Thirty-nine per cent of all the poor children in this region are under the age of six.
Government Orders
We know that poverty leads to higher death rates among children, more accidents, higher hospitalization rates, higher suicide rates, higher rates for dropping out of school, higher rates for never having a decent chance or a fair chance in life.
Child welfare graduates are over-represented among street youth; those on social assistance; the unemployed; the underemployed; those in juvenile prostitution, in youth courts and in penal institutions; and the learning disabled. There are thousands of kids as young as 13 who make their home on Canadian streets. They lead lives marked by poverty, disease, violence and crime.
When I was dealing with youth employment and training programs a few years ago, we were finding shocking statistics among young people who qualified for government training assistance, i.e. people who had been unemployed at least six months and with grade 10 or less education. They had no real employment history and therefore were eligible to come into training.
What we were finding consistently in these training programs was that 80 per cent or more of the young people who met those criteria had been victims of abuse. We can start to see the tremendous cost not only to the child but in actual dollars to society.
Among the prison population that is equally true. There is a very high rate of children who come from families marked by abuse such as substance abuse and direct sexual or physical abuse of the children.
The Liberal Party does not believe in going soft on young offenders. We do believe in trying to deal with the problem that put the young offender in the system in the first place and in not putting that young offender back into society as a danger to society and himself or herself. We have proposed lengthening the maximum sentence from three years to seven years to respond to evidence that the rehabilitative process can often take much longer than three years.
We believe that appropriate sentencing is necessary to maximize the chances of recovering a young life rather than dooming the young person and society to one more criminal on the streets. We have urged the government to establish a totally separate youth justice system in which sentencing and rehabilitation are all part of the package and to put in place the rehabilitative programs that are essential to achieving the objectives of both protecting society and giving the young offender a second chance.

Government Orders
Crime among youth is escalating. Society is paying a high cost for neglecting its most vulnerable and damaged young. These are the ones who end up as our young offenders. The young people who come into the justice system as criminals, and often as very violent criminals, have been failed throughout their youth and childhood by our society. If we fail at the point when they come into the system to deal with a problem that we have been neglecting then we lose the last chance society has to help young offenders become productive citizens.
Let us not miss the last chance we have when they are in trouble with the law, when we have the ability to put them in a controlled environment for their own good and for the protection of society.
The goal of the safe law abiding society rests not in abandoning the goal of recovering young lives but in working harder to achieve it.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take my place in this particular debate. I would like to start by complimenting the previous speaker who was in my opinion focused frankly on specific areas that need to be mentioned. I heartily endorse her comments about rehabilitation.
Thirty years ago I came into public life after having been dismissed from my job as a senior personnel officer in the corrections branch in the province of British Columbia for making public speeches on this very subject. I was told that I was outside government policy. From the experience of being dismissed from my job and with my professional background in this particular field I went on to become a politician, only to discover that like everybody else my priority in terms of dealing with children in trouble was not a high priority.
Little did I think that 30 years later the same arguments which were presented would still be necessary in other jurisdictions in this country. This bill is a knee-jerk reaction to what the government thinks is the need to get tough with law and orderissues.
Let me say at the outset that I do not believe there is any ill will in the government's attempt at this bill, but
frankly it is simply playing politics with the community and pandering to the lowest common denominator about what this issue is in depth. While my colleague talked about rehabilitation, I only have a few brief moments to concentrate on prevention.
We can predict at this point that regardless of this bill, in spite of this bill and some may partially argue because of this bill, there will be an increase in repeat crimes by young offenders. This is despite any work at all being done to prevent what we know are the seedlings and the fertile ground for future offenders in this country.
This bill does not address what my colleague touched on as a major part of the problem, that is poverty and neglect among children in this country. Frankly, and I say this from a moral perspective, it is immoral if not amoral that this government and previous governments of different political stripes have never set about establishing a child's charter in this nation to ensure that every young child, boy or girl, is defended in the face of every legal protection so that we can assure that each succeeding generation has done its best to prevent the kind of problems that we exacerbate by the nature of the society we have.
Is it justified that children go to school hungry? It is not just a trite statement to be made and abandoned because we are talking about this bill. The reality is that because of government policies, both provincially and federally, every single day children in this country go to school hungry. Every single day children go to school without adequate parental guidance or adult love. Children go to school in this country neglected and battered every single day.
What are the preventative programs to deal with these issues? They are not spoken by the government. They are not detailed out of committee, but instead we have another foolish bill that suggests that we can solve these problems by punishing children. It is very easy to punish children. There is a hypocrisy in our society. Children get punished far more readily by our court system than adults do. The cynicism around the treatment of adults in our criminal justice system, particularly if you are rich, does not even translate down to children.
November 21, 1991

The quality of the lawyer and the kind of money you have to back you up in the criminal justice system have a major impact on whether you are going to be convicted or found innocent.
Even that range is diminished because for the most part wealthy children do not show up in incarceration. It is the children of poverty and the children of neglect whom we focus on through this kind of legislation with some kind of campaign suggesting law and order and that we are going to show the community we are protecting it.
Every single child who is in need of preventative care and does not get it because of the absence of decent food, decent clothing and decent housing is a ticking time bomb and will come back to haunt the community as adult offenders.
I want to point out that it is not as if we do not know who these children are. Let us examine the first line of defence if we want to talk about protecting the community from violent offenders. From early childhood years we can demonstrate right at the kindergarten or school level the need for preventative services for children who are already giving us signals about severe problems and disturbance.
Tell me where across this country there is a concentrated, detailed preventative program available in the public school system that ensures that a child who shows up in that system, immediately spotted, has access to the kind of care, focus and attention that he or she needs. It cannot be done. That is not our concentration. We will spend money on incarcerating people. We will spend money on punishing people, but any sensible dollar to be spent on prevention is purely accidental rather than by national or provincial planning.
There is lip service being paid to this problem through the private agencies. Lord knows there are many United Way agencies that do attempt to provide preventative child care services, but we have always left that to the private sector. We have always assumed that charity would take care of "charity needs". We have never understood as a nation that our basic moral responsibility is to the child. That is a community responsibility not to be fobbed off in the hope of some charity dollar.
To suggest that this bill by punishing young offenders is going to solve the problem somehow is an outright lie. I am not naming anybody as a liar but the bill is a lie. The bill will leave the impression earnestly with some politi-
Govemment Orders
cians that once it is passed this problem is dealt with. That is a lie. The bill will leave the impression with the public that somehow we are making new moves to deal with juvenile crime. That is a lie. The bill will leave the impression with some journalists and some earnest editorial writers that this somehow is a step forward in dealing with a very serious problem. I say that is a lie.
As long as there are children hungry in this country, as long as there are children neglected in this country, sexually abused, physically abused and without one adult figure who is able to give love to that child, these problems will continue to grow and expand exponentially in our greatly growing anonymity in our society.
In the old days there was a role for the religious communities in dealing with these kinds of problems. This too has broken down. We are talking about the anonymity of a neglected child in a community that frankly does not give a damn. To suggest that somehow we are going to protect that child from becoming a violent offender by these meagre moves in this bill is absolutely stupid.
What can be done? Let us quickly and in a forthright manner examine a serious problem about poverty. Let us commit ourselves as a nation to say that no child shall ever go to school hungry again. Let us commit ourselves to say that no child, regardless of where he or she lives in this nation, should ever be forced to live in hovels or abandoned to the kind of housing that is a national disgrace, let alone an international disgrace. Let us commit ourselves to a preventative social and health care program that ensures that every aspect of society's services can be mobilized for those children in need.
I am not talking about the 98 per cent or 99 per cent of children who have the good fortune, regardless of all the other inhibitions, to have some loving relationship in their life that can sustain them even through poverty and bad housing.
I am talking about that 1 per cent or even 2 per cent of the children who have never had a chance from the moment they have been bom. For those groups-and I throw this in with a note of sincerity-that claim to be the great advocates as anti-abortionists and the pro-lifers, I admire them for their principles but I disagree with their position.

Government Orders
I challenge those groups. If they are so concerned about the lives of the unborn, let them be just as concerned about the ones who are bom and put the same amount of energy into defending those children, the kinds of rights they have and the kinds of services they have.
Thirty years have gone by and I still have to make this kind of speech. This indicates to me that either I am a failure or nobody has been listening. But I am not alone; I am not alone. Just recently in this community of Ottawa there were over 400 men and women from all types of organizations demanding of us parliamentarians a new and broad understanding of children's needs in this country.
All of our caucuses met with those people and we were all pious with our platitudes with those people. The summation after their arriving in Ottawa is that we are all good men and women regardless of party, dedicated to the needs of children. It is not true.
It is not because this Parliament is indifferent. It is not because the politicians are indifferent. Frankly we have never taken the time to understand what the heck these problems are in the first place. It is not because they are Tories, Liberals or New Democrats. It simply is that we have not begun to understand that a dollar of prevention is worth $100 of rehabilitation. A dollar prevention is worth a lifetime of a secure life, chance or opportunity for every child in this country.
The only way we can do that in law is to pass a law guaranteeing a charter of rights for children in this country so that any time a child is hungry, without adequate housing or without necessary services in terms of prevention, then by law they are entitled to receive those by order of a court. Anything less will not work.
The goodness, the good will, the decency of all of us collectively simply will not work because priorities around budgets at the municipal level, the provincial level and the federal level are always squeezed for other needs.
Children come first. We can all mouth that, but we have to go beyond it and enshrine it in law to ensure that we are beginning to deal with these problems.
I know I have conveyed with some modest passion some opinions to my colleagues here today and that the
government will withdraw the bill and say: "We are going to redirect our energies to ensure that children are protected". Would that happen, I would be a very happy person.
But I would walk out of here. I have said my peace and this day will go. The same system that creates child criminal offenders will go on and on and on with somehow believing that we have done something today to stop it. It is simply not true.
There are my comments. If we really love children, if we really care for children, then let us do it by backing it up with law, not with claptrap.

Madam Speaker, the Young Offenders Act and its amendments raise a subject dear to a number of members of Parliament, I include the one who just spoke as well as myself and I am sure there are many others.
The real point is: What do we do to resolve the problem in Canada of abused and neglected children? How do we martial the legislative and governmental forces to resolve that problem? I think that parliamentary histrionics will not in any way contribute to the resolution of the problem.
I am sure, my hon. friend agrees that we have to be workmanlike about the business of constructing a model legislatively and through governmental resources to respond to the problem.
I hope the member realizes that the Young Offenders Act and its implementation across Canada deal with one aspect of the child abuse and neglect problem and that is the child who runs afoul of the criminal laws. The laws that are there are designed to protect all other citizens. We have to deal with that problem in a real world and in a real way.
I want to ask the member about his interest in the Canadian charter of rights for children. For many years in this House of Commons and other places I have advocated the cause of missing children and sought legislation to deal with that problem. I have been told by officials in the Department of Justice that we cannot deal with the problem federally. We cannot include it in our criminal law because that power was left to the provinces under the civil law power to enact laws to protect neglected and abused children.
November 21, 1991

The member advocates this Canadian charter of rights for children. I would like to ask him how he proposes to implement that. How does he propose to get the provinces and the federal government onside? Does he recognize that we need a constitutional base for doing this? How are we going to do this unless we succeed in the constitutional initiatives of providing a proper and expedient method for amending the Constitution so that we can overcome these problems?
I say to the member as well: Will he ask his friend, the new premier of British Columbia, to take up this cause and to seek a charter of rights for children and initiate legislation in his own legislature that will lead to a constitutional amendment?

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for raising these questions.
The obstacles are not as insurmountable as one would think, as they appear on the surface. For example, let me give a parallel program. One single province initiated socialized medicine in this country and then it ultimately became federally mandated with federal conditions on it. As a matter of fact it was Madam Begin's own legislation that even told the provinces what they could not do about socialized medicine. What is there is the power of the province and then the federal government to order things to be done.
Second, it is already a fact that every province constitutionally has the power to apprehend a child. Every province in this country is mandated by law to apprehend a neglected child, if the complaint is verified, and to protect that child, even removing the child from its parents and putting the child in a foster home. We have mandated the provinces to make those decisions in intervention.
I say that the power is already there. There is not one province that would go back on a foster care program. There is not one province that would go back on the authority to apprehend a child. There is not one province that would deny its responsibility in ensuring, once the case is made in front of a juvenile court, that the child receive the care.
Government Orders
What I am saying is that we should go the next step as we tried to do in British Columbia by closing both Brannen Lake and Willingdon School for girls. We closed them. We ordered them closed, never to return again in the same form, those two training schools. All it takes is leadership and courage.
I am suggesting the legislative pattern that exists in this country would provide it. I say to the member: "Don't walk out, but come back and name a province that does not have this authority already". The authority and the leadership the member asked for exist today in every single province. What is lacking is the will or the commitment to add the auxiliary services.
It is true that the authority to seize a child by the state is already there, but once the child is seized by the state what is the moral and social obligation of the state to provide the services that are necessary? An adult cannot be seized in the same way. The state cannot seize an adult in the same way as it seizes a child. This is a serious responsibility. If the member is serious, he would make sure that the fiscal policies and the budgetary means are there to ensure that child receives the nourishment both emotional and physical which he or she needs. To fob it off by saying that some premier should do something is at best a misguided notion of what already exists. We have the authority. We just do not have the will to commit the budgets.

Madam Speaker, I would like to compliment my fellow colleague on his tremendous speech. If there is a time for outrage then I suggest this is a prime time for it.
I would like to ask the member a question on the basis of his tremendous experience in this field and leading out of a comment I heard Jesse Jackson make actually a year or so ago. He said: "You have two choices:"-maybe four but in groups of two-"you can have child care now or you can have jail care and welfare later". Although it may not be exactly within the context of the bill, I wonder if the member could make a bit of a connection between the neglect of our children and the ultimate problems we have in later years with criminality.

November 21, 1991
Government Orders

I want to thank the member for his comment. It is like that popular commercial: "You can pay me now or pay me later".
If we want to look at it purely as taxpayers' dollars, every shred of evidence shows that prevention saves money. But to go a bit further, where there have been studies, where every effort has been made at preventative care at an early age, the preventative intervention has shown that violence will diminish, that person to person attacks will diminish, and that a productive, mature adult is produced in society.
How does it make sense? The member wants an analogy. I will finish by giving an analogy. If a well is poisoned it is obvious that the water has to be cleaned up, so we move immediately under public health and clean up the water. If an illness is diagnosed early and we get preventative treatment then we save a life. There are poisoned wells out there that we know exist, and they are poverty, bad housing, and neglect of children by not having proper day care. Those are the poisoned wells.
There are problems of infection with the same medical analogy. We can spot a virus very early in a youngster. It may be sociological, not physical, but it is real just the same. When we prevent that, just as we do with inoculation or preventative care, we also give preventative medicine. The analogies are there.

Madam Speaker, I am very delighted to have the opportunity today to address the House of Commons with the concerns that my constituents have brought to me about the Young Offenders Act and about the society that produces offences by young people.
I want to begin my remarks by just saying that the riding I represent, Scarborough West, is one of five federal ridings in the city of Scarborough, which has a population of 550,000. That is a sizeable population. Within my riding I have a sizeable population both of youth and of senior citizens. In the city of Scarborough, and particularly in the riding of Scarborough West, we have conflict and we have difficulty. Some of the conflict and difficulty involves young people who may or may not be dealt with by the legislation we are talking about today.
Very recently in my riding, or just north of my riding actually, literally across the street, there was an incident
on a Sunday at a flea market which was packed with people. A group of approximately 50 youths in an obviously well organized, well planned raid, stormed into the flea market, destroyed the glass panels of a jewellery vendor and stole over $100,000 worth of jewellery, almost like a military operation, and they were gone before anyone could even react.
A street in my riding is called Leyton Avenue. People literally are living in fear. In fear of what? In fear of drugs. There are crack houses on that street. It is a known hang-out for some elements of youth. People are afraid to walk on that street. People are literally afraid to walk by certain of the houses on that street. The efforts of the police, while laudable, have not been able to stem the problem. Safety in the streets has been affected.
I am not overdramatizing when I say that the sister of one of my constituency assistants literally had to dive for cover and cover her child with her own body on Leyton Avenue because of gun play. This is in the riding of Scarborough West in the city of Scarborough, in the province of Ontario, in the country of Canada.
If you wear shoes called Doc Martins, or if you have a leather jacket, or indeed any kind of expensive apparel and you are a young person or you are elderly, you literally have to think not twice but three or four times before you go to a local shopping mall. Before you leave that local shopping mall, you may have been swarmed and you may have no jacket and you may have no shoes. The majority of those offences are being committed by young people.
That is a tragedy. People do not seem to know what to do about it. People seem unable to grasp what has happened. They have come to me and said: "What can you as the federal member do? What can Parliament do? What will Parliament do? Is anybody listening? Does anybody know that this is happening in our country?"
I have held public forums in my riding on the topic of safety in the streets and on the Young Offenders Act. I have requested that people write to me about their concerns. I want to tell you, Madam Speaker, that they have attended these forums and they have written to me. I now have the opportunity as their representative to state to this House what their concerns are and what they want me to tell the House of Commons.
November 21, 1991

There are a number of concerns but the first one is protection for themselves. They feelthat they are no longer able to walk from the senior citizens' home to the local Becker's store and back home. They are confined to their apartments because they fear for their own lives. This is in a major metropolitan area of our country. It is hard to believe but it is the fear.
Virtually everyone I am afraid as a result of this fear feels that the present Young Offenders Act, and I use their words, is "too lenient". We talk about that. We tiy to understand what too lenient means. Of course, we are talking here not about adults but about children. We are talking about young people who in many cases come from broken families with terrible stories of abuse and difficulty. What do we do? I have heard that in cases of serious offences people want transfer to adult court to be made easier. Why? For the protection of society. These cases are not frequent but when they happen, they shock the sensibilities.
In Scarborough there was a youth who killed three people. He received three years. He is now out on the street. Three years for three lives. That is unacceptable to the people of Scarborough West.
What about the jurisdiction of the Young Offenders Act? People in my riding have pointed out, and I should point it out as well, that the Young Offenders Act of course replaces the Juvenile Delinquents Act. The Juvenile Delinquents Act was drafted in another time, when we did not have the knowledge that we have now about human psychology and about the growth of human beings throughout their lifetimes. However, the age at which a person was responsible was seven years of age. It has now been raised to twelve. That is a concern, as I will illustrate later.
The final concern that was brought out unanimously,was the inability to publish the names of people charged with serious offences. This is not just pointed out by residents and the constituents of Scarborough West; this is pointed out by the metropolitan Toronto police force. How difficult it is for them to apprehend alleged offenders if it cannot identify those alleged offenders to the public. If someone is alleged to have committed a sexual assault on a 10-year old girl, and the police know who they are looking for, they cannot identify that young person. It is against the law. That hampers the ability of the police to apprehend that
Government Orders
young person and bring him in to the system which we all hope is going to be able to help to bring him back into society as a productive member. So they are concerned about the ability to publish these names, and this affects their safety.
What is the approach of the Young Offenders Act to young persons? I think it is worth while to quote directly from section 3 of the act, and I quote;
It is hereby recognized and declared that (a) while young persons should not in all instances be held accountable in the same manner or suffer the same consequences for their behaviour as adults, young persons who commit offences should nonetheless bear responsibility for their contraventions.
That is in the act.
(b)	Society must, although it has the responsibility to take reasonable measures to prevent criminal conduct by young persons, be afforded the necessary protection from illegal behaviour.
(c)	Young persons who commit offences require supervision, discipline and control but, because of their state of dependency and level of development and maturity, they also have special needs and require guidance and assistance.
There are a number of other sections, but I am only going to go as far as subsection 3(d).
(d)	Where it is not inconsistent with the protection of society, taking no measures or taking measures other than judicial proceedings under this act should be considered for dealing with young persons who have committed offences.
I do not quarrel with those general statements. The constituents of Scarborough West, I believe, do not quarrel with those general statements. It is the application of those general statements that has brought some problems, and I would like to talk specifically about three of them.
What about transfer to adult court for serious offences? That is one of the things that this bill, the amendment to the Young Offenders Act, is talking about. What is the purpose? Is the purpose to force the young person who is alleged to have committed the serious act-let us say it is murder-into the adult system? Is it the purpose that upon conviction they should go into an adult penal institution? No, I do not believe so. I believe the purpose is to ensure that on a finding of guilt, for the protection of society and for the betterment of the young person who can then take advantage of counselling and all of the other programs that hopefully would be provided by society, society would be protected and we would be prevented from having a sentence of only three years for the crime of murder.

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
Does this bill do that? The government would have us believe it is are responding to this concern of society, but I say no, this bill does not do that. What it does, sadly, is pretend to do that. If a young person is found guilty of first degree murder or second degree murder in youth court, the bill provides for a maximum sentence of five years, as opposed to the present three years. Or does it? If you look at the bill, you will see that the clause amends the present provision to provide that the person will be ordered "to serve a disposition not to exceed five years less a day". If we left it at that, that would seem fairly obvious on its face. However, it goes on:
-comprised of
(i)	a committal to custody, to be served continuously, for a period that shall not, subject to subsection 26.1.(1), exceed three years from the date of committal, and
(ii)	a placement under conditional supervision to be served in the community in accordance with section 26.2.
What does that mean? That means that if we pass this act, a young person who commits the offence of murder will still go to jail for a maximum of three years, no more, if they are found guilty in youth court. Then they will be placed under "conditional supervision" for a period of a further two years.
Really, there is no increase for the protection of society to five years. There is no ability of society to be able to exercise the degree of control necessary for someone who has taken a human life to be able to rehabilitate that person beyond three years, and yet the government pretends that it is responding to the concerns of Canadians for further protection.
What happens if a young person is convicted in adult court? First of all, I am sure that most right thinking people would agree that no young person should be thrown into jail with hardened criminals who are adults. This is not logical. This will not benefit either the young person or, in the long term, society at large.
But what happens? If a person is found guilty, and this could be just as easily a person who is one day short of 18 as a person who is one day past the age of 14, the bill provides that the sentence is life imprisonment without eligibility for parole for between 5 and 10 years, as specified by the judge. If an adult is found guilty, he must serve between 10 and 25 years.
What does that mean? It means that in the particular case that we are talking about, where the young person killed three people-that person was 17 and a half when those murders were committed-the maximum penalty, if that person had been taken to adult court, which that person was not, would have been under this bill a maximum of 10 years, if so specified by the judge.
That is not acceptable to the people of Scarborough West.
What about the jurisdiction of this bill? Many people might not realize that young person is defined as "anyone who is 12 years of age up to 18". What does that mean? That means that if you are under the age of 12, this act does not apply to you. It absolutely does not apply if you are under the age of 12.
In today's paper, there was an incident in Toronto where an 11-year old child had a metal replica of a gun, and that young person, who is not a young person for the purposes of the Young Offenders Act, pistol-whipped an elderly citizen. The police apprehended that 11-year-old and they are powerless to do anything except return that young person back into the hands of the Children's Aid Society. This act does absolutely nothing to help those young people who are under the age of 12 and who get involved in breaches of the law.
If this is known by me, if this is known by my constituents, it is positively known by drug dealers. It is positively known by adults why prey on children and who will use them and have already used them in the United States and in parts of Canada to be couriers for drugs, to be their mules, knowing that because they are under the age of 12 absolutely nothing can be done. This bill does nothing to deal with that problem, and that is a concern that society has. We passed a bill on gun control but if an 11-year old child is seen walking down the street with a handgun obtained from his parents' cupboard, or wherever, nothing can be done. Yes, the gun can be confiscated and given back to the parent but nothing can be done to that 11-year old child. Is that logical? The people of Scarborough West do not believe so. That is the tragedy as well because those young people cannot be helped.
November 21, 1991

As the section says, those young people require supervision, discipline and control, but they cannot get it because they are not dealt with by the Young Offenders Act.
There is absolutely no change brought about by these amendments with respect to the publication of the names of people who are alleged to have committed serious criminal offences. That is a major flaw. The people of Canada want to know that they are protected, want to know that when their children go to school there is no one among them who has been charged or convicted of a serious criminal offence. We can argue about a definition of serious. I am talking about first or second degree murder.
These are some of the problems that have been identified by my constituents. By no means is it of all of them. What irritates me as their representative, and them is the attempt by this government to pretend that it is dealing with their concerns, when all it is doing is putting out a little bit of window dressing around Christmastime to try and convince Canadians that something is being done.
Young people are not being helped and the concerns of society are not being listened to. I say it is time to listen, not only to the bureaucrats, not only to the so-called experts, but also to Canadians who are afraid to walk the streets, Canadians who feel frustrated that no one is listening, to young people who cry out for authority and guidance in an age when the watchwords are: "Do your own thing "and" if it feels good, do it". We cannot continue with that.
We must come to grips with the fundamental problems that are besetting us, attacks on the family and attacks on authority. It is time to identify these concerns. This bill or the act is a tool which can be used to protect our society and help our wayward children. Let us treat the wound instead of debating the size and colour of the bandage. This bill does not treat the wound and I will be voting against it.

Madam Speaker, I had the opportunity to be sitting here just a few moments ago before this hon. member spoke to listen to the speech of the hon. member for Esquimau-Juan de Fuca who spoke so eloquently about
Government Orders
prevention and the need for young people to be spared poverty and deprivation in our society.
I listened to the hon. member who just spoke and I wonder if he understood the words of the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca on preventive matters. When the member speaks about an 11-year old child engaged in a violent activity or an 11-year old child walking down the street waving a handgun, I wonder if the member is suggesting that something has to be done to punish that 11-year, old child who may have engaged in violent activity, or does he recognize that 11-year old child requires help. That 11-year old child may have been living in overcrowded housing conditions and may have been denied food and sustenance, may have been denied attention, love and care at home. Must that 11-year old child be punished for the way in which society has dealt with him, or does that 11-year old child need care and attention? Should he or she be brought into our society and assured that the child fits into our society?
Is prevention important to the hon. member who just spoke? Or do we have to deal with law and order, throw them in jail, throw away the key, and they have to pay the price for their sins?

Madam Speaker, I really do wonder if the member was listening when I spoke.
I indicated my full support for section 3(c) of the Young Offenders Act which quite plainly says that young people are not adults and require special guidance and assistance which adults do not get.
The point however is that 11-year old child will not get the special guidance and help that society can give because that 11-year old child is not covered by the Young Offenders Act. That is the point.
We are not talking about punishing an 11-year old child. We are talking about helping an 11-year old child, and, yes, I did listen very carefully to the hon. member from Juan de Fuca.
I agree that we have to look at the problems of society and we have to deal with this problem in an over-all sense. I ask hon. members to consider, at a time when the family is under attack, when people are ridiculed for promoting the concept of two-parent families with both parents providing love, care and guidance, when people are ridiculed for advocating monogamous heterosexual relationships, when pornography is proliferating under the guise of freedom of expression, when we are killing

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
over 100,000 unborn children, female and male, each year at taxpayer expense, at a time when segments of western society are talking about the active killing of the weak and infirm, when males assault females in ever growing numbers and when women and children are abused for sexual gratification, is it any wonder that Canadians feel that our society is falling apart?
Yes, we have to deal with all these matters. We cannot deal with something in isolation and we certainly cannot deal with a bill that pretends to be something it is not.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to speak again on this particular piece of legislation, to discuss in general the wrong aim of the government's bill, to address some of the concerns that I think all members of society have as they relate to young offenders and also to discuss some of the issues that have already been discussed here this morning.
The Liberal Party will not be supporting this legislation because we do not think it works. We recognize there are problems. I had an experience just last evening.
It is hard to believe but I was babysitting for my brother. One of my nephews was asking me about my son, what he does in school and things like that. Patrick also asked me whether he had any Doc Martins, which are the shoes that kids wear these days. I said that yes, he did have a pair. I thought they were the worst looking pair of shoes I had ever seen but he thinks they are kind of neat.
Patrick told me that if he could get those shoes, he could not wear them to school because someone would take them from him. I listened to that and really had trouble believing that was the shape of things until you hear some of the stories about violence in our schools and violence among our youth.
I know my own son, Stephen, talks about attacks among his friends and unprovoked attacks against some of his friends. There is violence and police involvement and all of those things. As we have grown up, I think we have all faced some difficult situations but most of the time, it seems to me-maybe I was sneaky enough or cowardly enough that I always managed to avoid those confrontations-today these confrontations occur more often.
We do have problems with youth and you hear stories of the real crime elements, of drug lords utilizing youth as part of that trade. You hear of youths being involved
in swarmings and all of those types of things. We recognize that there are problems.
I guess my concern is that I am not sure that locking up children is the way to solve that particular problem. I agree with some of the comments just made, that we have to take a look at this on an holistic basis. There are housing problems. There is poverty. There is child abuse that leads to these types of circumstances. Are we really treating the symptoms rather than treating the actual cause?
This legislation and the changes that are proposed by the government are still just treating symptoms and not moving to the real root cause of the problem. How do we eradicate poverty and youth poverty? How do we eradicate the problems of housing and situations like that? How do we eradicate child abuse? Those are things that have to be addressed as well.
I believe that this legislation will do nothing really to solve that problem. What it is responding to in large measure is the issue of law and order, keeping these kids off our streets and locked up and out of the way. I think that in some sense we can understand that because we do not like to see that type of violence occurring in our communities and we particularly do not like to see it where it involves young people.
At the same time, locking up a child for 10, 15 or 20 years like an adult is going to create, in my view, a monster in the end. If we take the classic case of a youth who was involved in murder, transfer that youth to adult court and put that youth in an adult prison for 20 years, what are we going to have? The thing to remember is that child is probably 15, 16 or maybe 17. Tack that 20 years on and we are looking at someone who is going to be back in society at age 35, 36 or 37 and what have we created with that youth?
In my opinion, Madam Speaker, and I am sure that you would agree, we have created a monster. We will create a number of monsters because our prison system is such that if those children were abused before they went to prison, for sure they will be abused while they are there. We will then be condoning that abuse of our youth.
I think the intent of the young offenders legislation is proper. We should say that youth are different and we should look at how we treat youth and how we make them pay for the mistakes that they make. We have to look at a whole host of things.
November 21, 1991

However, making it too easy to transfer young offenders into the adult system is not in my way of thinking rightly aimed. The obvious situation is that if you are unfortunate enough to be a youth in some provinces you are more likely to be transferred to the adult system than if you are in another province. I cannot remember the statistics exactly but I know that you are less likely to be sent to an adult court in Prince Edward Island than you are in Manitoba.
A youth or a child is going to have his life dictated somewhat by where he or she lives. That is not fair and equal treatment under the law. We must have as much even treatment as possible in our system so that all youths are treated fairly and equally.
The other complaint that I see in the legislation and the concern that I have is in the area of rehabilitation, training and education. For a child of 14 to 15 to turn to crime means that something very seriously wrong has occurred prior to attaining that age. What are we doing to rehabilitate, train and educate these children?
I guess our answer is: Let us send them to the adult prison and there they can get their education and they can learn how to make licence plates. The legislation does not seem to be rightly aimed in my view. They can learn how to perform crime better in this adult institution. They can learn how to avoid being caught the next time they get out rather than sending them to institutions and places where we can try to convince them that life or that lifestyle is one that is unacceptable and not to be accepted by society and at the same time point them in a direction that they do not see the benefits of crime and in fact they see nothing but the disadvantages of crime. The opportunities that our society presents to them are such that they can be participants in society.
Instead the government is of the view that we should make it easier for these children to be sent off to the adult institutions. We have all heard the gruesome stories and we might as well say them out loud. Some of the older prisoners look with glee when young boys arrive at that institution. They are even carving up the spoils, so to speak. What this government wants to do is send those children to that life, to that lifestyle.
We on this side of the House feel that is wrong. We feel it contradicts the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, and while the government has tried to fix it up
Government Orders
it has failed. That contradiction of the UN charter of Rights still exists and has not been dealt with.
We believe that the solution to achieving the intent of the legislation-and the intent is good-is a thorough overhaul of the whole system to create a youth system of justice. Let us keep youth in that system.
There is no question that some youths are abusing the system as it presently exists. I do get upset when people talk about the child who committed three murders and only got three years. That was not the fault of the legislation. It was the fault of the court, and the people who administered it. We cannot strike down the intent and direction of that legislation just because it has not been properly handled.
We think that two things have to be done. There has to be a youth or juvenile system with all of the rehabilitation, training and education facilities that are necessary so that we can salvage these youths. At the same time there have to be some deterrents. Those presently in the legislation do not seem to be working. In my other life as mayor of a community I would listen to the police talk of the problems of juvenile crime and try to solve those problems. I am aware of the problems that the police forces face.
But the solution that the police want is a longer sentence. I think in some sense that is not bad, depending on what we are going to do with that child or that youth. Maybe we should look at it as an opportunity to try to salvage that youth and not put him out of the way in an institution so we do not have to worry about him for a period of time. If we do that we are going to have to worry about him when that period of time is over. We will face far more serious problems each time we do that.
Maybe we should get our house in order as far as youth are concerned. We must deal with a proper housing policy. We must deal with poverty in our inner cities and poverty among youth and elderly people, all of those things. We have to look at all of these issues on an holistic basis.
We on this side think that the present legislation is wrong. We proposed a number of amendments that would have put some heart into the legislation and corrected many of the deficiencies that are there so that it would comply with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. But the government did not see that as a good idea. It decided to move on the side of punishment

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
rather than on the side of salvaging youth. For us on this side of the House that is unacceptable.

Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague has indeed touched on many of the pertinent points with regard to this legislation. The whole theme of what he was saying this morning was that we should look at ways to salvage youth rather than simply punish them.
I share with him and many parents across Canada the grave malaise we have in this country. Young offenders seem to snub their noses at the system. As recently as a week ago I had a call from a mother who was saying that because of the way the law is interfering with her life she has less and less control over her children. She was asking me how she was going to raise her children. I bring this point up only to show that she wants to salvage them, but at this point it seems that the law puts her children beyond her.
My colleague has mentioned that we should have the proper facilities and training. I very strongly believe that we should have mandatory counselling whenever a young offender is charged and convicted and before he is released. I do not believe that they should have the option of whether they take this counselling or not. This opens the door once again to the young offender saying: "Look, I do not want to be helped". In many cases I do not know if they are equipped to make that decision.
I put it squarely to my colleague. I would very much like him to make not only a personal comment but one on behalf of the Liberal Party as he is our direct spokesperson in this debate. I would like his views on what I think is a necessity at this point, that is the obligatory counselling of young offenders after they have been accused, after they have been tried and after they have been sentenced for crimes which they have committed.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question. It was one of the difficult issues that our committee faced when we looked at this particular legislation. What is suggested by compulsory training and rehabilitation is overshadowed by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and whether those rights exist and how we could accomplish that.
Our view on the committee was that we probably could not make it compulsory, even though some of us thought that it was a good idea and would like to do it. The advice that we received was that it would be struck down as unconstitutional. We thought that if we put enough flexibility into the system we could probably achieve the goal by using the carrot and stick method. Youth who took the training, rehabilitation, counselling and all of those types of things would be eligible for consideration for being out sooner. More benefits would flow to that young person by embarking on a rehabilitation-type process through consultation and those types of measures.
The other answer that I would like to give to my colleague is that the problem we face in Canada is that we are told we do not have enough resources. That is the scary part of this legislation and the way the government is aiming it. Its solution is to bump them up into adult court, just get rid of them, and then we will not have to face that problem.
What we are saying on this side of the House is: put the money to the test and make a system that works. Let us have a youth system with all of the benefits that could flow from that. Let us keep our youth out of the adult system. Make all of the consultations, rehabilitation, education and training facilities available so we can salvage our youth.
In short, my answer is that I personally thought that compulsory treatment and counselling was a good idea, but I faced the legal argument of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I had to agree that probably would intrude on the situation and therefore we could not achieve what might be a good idea.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his excellent speech.
I think it gave us a lot of information and certainly put in perspective, first of all, the problems that this bill creates and, second, the problems that are already there that it does not help.
The member has alluded to the fact that we will send these young people to incarceration and they will come out after having had a crash course in how to commit crime. They will also be sexually and physically abused so there will be a greater than average chance that they will
November 21, 1991

have a terrible grudge against society. They will feel that now they have made this start in life they cannot possibly recoup, and they will just continue what they are doing and become more desperate and proficient at doing it.
I think we are not solving anything here with respect to rehabilitation and treatment of the young offender. I do not think we are doing anything to curb the increasing crime rate in this country that has alarmed a great many of our citizens.
I would just like to ask the hon. member who represents a community in Atlantic Canada and has been involved in municipal government about his concerns and the concerns of his citizens with respect to the rising crime rate. We have heard about the concern of citizens in large cities and I just want to ask him if that concern also applies to average or medium sized cities.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question. I do not think there is any question that all communities throughout Canada are concerned about the rising crime rate. That is what we have to be on our guard against, and because it is occurring we have a knee-jerk reaction.
I think we have to put in place a system that will work. I was just reading a comment in one of the recent media reports that violence by youth rose by 34 per cent over a four-year period and that violent crime was up dramatically in the year 1990-91.
There is no question that there is a problem and it is not only in the big cities. In my own community we have seen a number of violent crimes and an increase in the number of murders. That even excludes the high profile ones like Allen Legere and others that everybody has heard about.
In the youth area, as we talk to school teachers and parents, we recognize that there is an upswing in violence among youths. The children in our schools are living to a degree in fear and have now learned how to deal with the rules of the jungle.
My nephew Patrick told me last night that he would never wear any clothes that were in style because somebody would try to take them. This is a kid who is 11 or 12 years old. That is the reality that a kid here in
Government Orders
Ottawa is dealing with, and my son tells me the same thing in Moncton, New Brunswick. It is a problem. There is violence and the children have learned how to deal with it. Patrick told me that he just wears regular stuff. He does not wear any of the popular things because that would be a problem.
There is violence. There are serious things happening. They are not just happening in the big cities; they are happening in the small cities too.

Government Orders CRIMINAL CODE

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-30, an act to amend the Criminal Code (mental disorder) and to amend the National Defence Act and the Young Offenders Act in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General.

Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to rise and speak in favour of this bill at third reading stage. I believe this bill represents a major improvement in the law respecting the mentally disordered who have come into conflict with the criminal law.
In introducing this bill the Minister of Justice said it proposes "wide-ranging changes to modernize, streamline and clarify the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with mentally disordered accused".
Today I would like to deal with the role of the review boards in assuring that mentally disordered persons who have been found to be either unfit to stand trial or not criminally responsible are dealt with fairly and in a manner that takes into account public safety.
Under the provisions of the Criminal Code as they stand today, the lieutenant-governor of the province is the person responsible for making all decisions regarding the detention, care and conditions of release of those under the authority of a lieutenant-governor's warrant. While the code does provide for the establishment of boards to review the cases of persons held in custody under a lieutenant-governor's warrant, this provision is not mandatory. British Columbia and the two territories have yet to establish review boards under the authority of the code. The role of the board is merely advisory. Nor
does the code give much guidance as to how boards should conduct themselves.
It is therefore not surprising that the Law Reform Commission of Canada in its report entitled Mental Disorder in the Criminal Process, published in 1976, found that the make-up of the boards differ, the resources available to the boards differ, the criteria they apply, the procedures they use, the material they examine and the rights they accord the prisoner patients all differ from province to province. In some the differences far exceed the similarities.
While in recent years the review boards have taken pains to find out what their counterparts in other provinces are doing, the first annual report, Canadian Data Base: Patients Held On Lieutenant-Governors' Warrants, prepared by Doctors Hodgins and Webster for the federal Department of Justice in October 1989, continued to show very considerable discrepancies in procedures.
I do not by this intend any criticism of the review boards or their members who are performing a difficult task with great dedication. Nor am I suggesting that we should insist upon absolute uniformity of procedure as between the various review boards. However it behoves us to assure that there is equality of justice in the way in which we treat mentally disordered persons who come into conflict with the criminal law. This is particularly so in light of the comments made by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case of Swain v. The Queen, which talks about the way in which mentally disordered individuals are dealt with presently under the Criminal Code.
In order to foster equality of treatment the bill requires that a review board be set up in each province and territory. This provision guarantees that no matter where one is in Canada cases of this type will be dealt with by a body that has the same structure, powers and obligations as elsewhere in the country. Moreover, henceforth the review board will be the decision-making body rather than merely an adviser to the lieutenant-governor as is the case today.
From both a legal and practical point of view this change makes sense. There is a principle of law that the person who decides the case must hear the evidence, but the lieutenant-governor presently hears neither the witnesses nor the arguments of counsel. It is the review board that sees the mentally disordered person, hears
November 21, 1991

the evidence, examines the files and has the expertise to make a proper assessment of what needs to be done.
From a practical point of view in the larger provinces if the lieutenant-governor were to consider each individual's case with the same care that the review boards do, he or she would have to spend almost full time examining and deciding these cases. Of necessity therefore the lieutenant-governor must rely on the recommendations of the review board. The proposed modification puts the decision-making powers where they belong.
This bill also proposes changes in the structure of the review boards. Under the existing provisions of the Criminal Code, a review board shall consist of a minimum three and a maximum of five members, at least two of whom shall be duly qualified psychiatrists entitled to engage in the practice of medicine under the laws of the province for which the board is appointed, and one member shall be a member of the bar of that province.
The new provisions would set the size of the review board at a minimum of five but with no maximum. The larger minimum is to bring a greater range of expertise to the board, while the elimination of the maximum is to allow for different panels of the board to be created in large provinces so that service on the board does not become too onerous for its members who have to take time off from their regular positions.
The membership of the review boards will also be changed. With the elimination of the role of the lieutenant-governor from the process, it was thought important to have the board chaired by a federally appointed judge, a retired judge or a person eligible to be appointed as a judge. This would help to ensure that the public would have confidence in the board. Provision is made however to permit the incumbent chairperson to complete his or her term of office so as not to interfere with the operations of an existing board.
This bill also reduces the minimum number of psychiatrists on the review board from two to one. However, where only one psychiatrist is named at least one other person must have training and experience in relation to mental health and be qualified by the laws of a province to practise medicine or psychology.
The reason for this reduction in the required number of psychiatrists is that in the territories and in some of
Government Orders
the smaller provinces it is often difficult to find two psychiatrists that have not been involved in the treatment of a mentally disordered person before the board.
For this same reason the bill only requires that the designated professional members of the review boards be qualified somewhere in Canada and not necessarily in the jurisdiction where the board is located.
Both the Law Reform Commission of Canada report which I have referred to earlier and the study done by Doctors Webster and Hodgins reveal that the review boards conduct their hearings in a fairly idiosyncratic manner. It is not essential that the procedure followed exactly the same procedure in every board. However there are some basic rules which must be adhered to if the procedure is to be "in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice", to use the words of section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The following are some of the rights that should be respected in all cases: the right to receive a notice of hearing, the right to be represented by council, the right to be present during the whole hearing unless there is a good reason for being excluded, the right to give evidence, and the right to examine or cross-examine witnesses.
These are among the primary procedural rules set out in the bill. Other rules protect the privacy of the mentally disordered. They require the board to keep records of the proceedings and to give reasons for its decisions. There are miscellaneous rules dealing with specific problems that may arise. It should be made clear, however, that it is not intended by these amendments to convert the review boards into courts. The first in the list of procedural rules set out in the bill is that subject to those rules hearings may be conducted in as informal a manner as is appropriate under the circumstances.
The bill also provided that any procedural irregularity in relation to a hearing does not affect the validity of the proceedings unless the accused suffers substantive prejudice. While some boards may fear that the procedure spelled out in the bill will cause the proceedings for them to become longer and more complex, it is reassuring to learn from the Hon. Mr. Justice Thomas Callon, chairman of the Lieutenant-Governor's Board of Review,

Government Orders
that his board has been following these rules without any difficulty for the last three years.
In addition to setting out a core of provisions relating to procedure before the review boards, the bill sets out the dispositions the boards may make and the powers they may exercise in carrying out their functions. These provisions are necessary because the boards will have in the future the decision-making power which to date has been exercised by the lieutenant-governor.
Among the remaining provisions regarding the review boards, there are two I would like to mention particularly, for each of them deals with a problem that exists in the present legislation. The first provision grants a right of appeal from a board's decision to the court of appeal of the province or territory in question. At present there is no right of appeal either from the recommendations of the review board or from the decision of the lieutenant-governor, although some relief may be obtained from a decision of the latter in certain cases by means of a prerogative writ. It is universally agreed that a right of appeal ought to exist in such cases and this bill therefore addressed a long-standing deficiency in the law.
The other provision addresses the issue of which review board will have jurisdiction to review the case of a person who has been transferred from one province to another. At present there does not appear to be agreement on the subject. The bill resolves the question by stating that the board of the receiving province will have jurisdiction over the person subject to any special agreements that may have been entered into by the attorneys-general of the respecting provinces.
In summary, the bill modernizes the present law and resolves a number of problems in relation to the care and administration of those who are either unfit to stand trial or not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder. It does so in a manner that respects the rights of the mentally disordered while protecting the security interests of the public.
Finally, it appears to satisfy the concerns expressed by the Supreme Court in the case of Swain v. The Queen. There is an additional provision that was suggested by the hon. member for Moncton and agreed to during the
legislative committee process that the provisions of this bill should be reviewed within five years.
That is something I think all hon. members should welcome. This is a complicated provision we are dealing with and I think it is appropriate that Parliament should revisit the subject after five years.
I believe five years would be a long enough period to give reasonable time for this bill to be implemented and reasonable time for us to be able to assess either its positive aspects or its weaknesses, if any.
I am pleased that too is a part of the bill. As I say, I am pleased that this bill has received the co-operation of the House as a whole and that it received the co-operation of hon. members when it was referred to a legislative committee.
As a result of those deliberations and all the work that has gone into preparing this, I encourage every member of the House to support this legislation which I think is both progressive and humanitarian.

While there are some hesitations and concerns which were brought forward during the committee study, we feel that given the present circumstances we will support the bill. I am sure some people are a little confused with the Swain decision and what it means. In effect, the Supreme Court of Canada did put us to a very strict timeframe and we have had to deal with that.
In fact, the government was forced to ask for an extension of time because our time ran out on November
