Suffice it to say, sometimes during the committee hearings everyone was totally confused as to what it meant and how it would be administered.
I think in actuality the legislation is not bad. It does deal with the problems that were talked about in the Swain decision and deals with lieutenant-governor warrants and their unconstitutionality.
I was pleased to put forward the amendment that would see us come back and take another look precisely for what I have just said, the problems that the committee faced, trying to grapple with the different issues. This will at least allow us to go back and correct the deficiencies once they become apparent.
I am sure there will be some, but over all the bill seems to do what it is intended to do and that is a proper thing. Much of the bill, as well, is going to be implemented relatively slowly and the parliamentary secretary has referred to all the difficulties and all the things that the bill is going to do.
We are going to see what will happen over a period of time. Hospitals are going to start with pilot projects and some aspects of the legislation will not be in effect for two to three years. That was why the amendment was crafted, so that a five-year period would see the bill come up for review.
There is one problem. I consulted with most of the ministers of justice and ministers of health of the provinces to see what was going on from their vantage point. There are some concerns that the effect of this legislation will cause problems for the provinces. We should be mindful of that.
In essence what is being said-and that is the way our Constitution works-is that dealing with the criminal law we turn to the federal jurisdictions but when we are dealing with health and care of people through the health care system they become the responsibility of the provinces. We are going to see a burden placed on provinces. We were concerned that there might be some unevenness in the delivery of that health care. Those issues were also of concern to us.
I just want to quote from a couple of letters that I received because they contain this common theme of uncertainty as far as the provinces are concerned. From my own home province of New Brunswick, the minister
Government Orders
of health, the hon. Russell King, wrote back to me and said: "With regard to the department of health and community services concerns, the service delivery system required to ensure the Supreme Court decision is upheld will need to be flexible in terms of providing services in both the community and in a hospital setting. The additional need for the province of New Brunswick to prove dangerousness will require mental health specialists familiar with the mental health and criminal justice system, a specialty not previously required in this province. The community component of this service will involve screening, assessment and treatment. Further, the hospital component of this service will need to be upgraded".
That gives a clear indication of some of the concerns that the minister of health for the province of New Brunswick has observed in reviewing the legislation. He does not say: do not do it. He just says recognize that this is going to create some problems for New Brunswick.
The same theme occurred in a letter that I received from the minister of justice and premier of the province of Prince Edward Island, Joseph Ghiz. He indicated to me that his province supports the changes but recognizes the shift to the provinces particularly in the area of treatment. He is concerned and says: "The amendments make no attempt to build in treatment as part of Parliament's response to the mentally disordered offender but leaves that issue entirely in provincial hands at a time when there is a great deal of controversy across Canada on the civil rights aspect of involuntary treatment. We would rather have seen specific treatment provisions in these amendments as they represent a very narrow and justifiable public safety infringement on civil rights in a manner ancillary to and flowing from the public interest in safety and prevention of crime".
From these quotes and from other letters which I have received from across the country, the provinces do have a concern. They realize that it is their obligation to provide for the mentally ill, but we are dealing with the criminal justice system as well as the mentally ill. That is going to create new responsibilities and new stresses and strains on the hospital situation, on community based services and all of those types of things that have an impact on provincial budgets.
While the federal government is a beneficiary in a way because it has now dealt with this relatively easily from its vantage point, there will be an onus and a responsibil-

ity passed on to the provinces, and the provinces are concerned.
That points to the benefit of the amendment which we proposed on this side of the House because we will be able to look back after five years and determine whether the provinces have been successful in changing and adapting to the effects of this legislation.

Madam Speaker, I rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party as justice critic to speak on this bill. I just want to add a few remarks to some of the comments that have been made by my hon. friends who have already spoken, the parliamentary secretary and the member for Moncton.
To take up one of the member's themes and to re-emphasize it a bit more, the public policy process in this bill has not exactly been a rousing success. The government left it up to the Supreme Court of Canada to force a change in the present insanity provisions of the Criminal Code. That is what we are talking about in Bill C-30, the issue of criminal insanity.
The government has had the bill since 1986. It has had a Law Reform Commission report since 1976. That means it has been sitting on its hands and was forced by the Supreme Court of Canada finally to act. That is not a very good way of doing legislation. This minister has been very slow with her legislation. It is only in the past little while after a lot of public pressure and pressure from the opposition, I might add, that some action has finally been produced. We had all talk and no action. Now we have some action and we are pleased about it.
Some of the principles that have to be emphasized I noticed the parliamentary secretary opened his speech with and I basically agree with him. We have to take into account public safety, the safety of citizens from people who are insane versus human rights. These people do have human rights under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, rights as Canadian citizens and as individual human beings.
Part of the reason for the Swain case-and I believe that is the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada that brought on this amended bill if I recollect it right-was that someone was given a pretty well indeterminate sentence, locked up for a long time for an assault charge. That does not ring right with people. That seems wrong. I think that is why there was some basic feeling that this system really was wrong in terms of human rights.
We have to balance human rights with the public safety. I was able to see this concretely when I met a few months ago in British Columbia with some people from the human rights committee of the B.C. Mental Health Association, led by a woman called Judy Shipper who came to Ottawa to testify before our parliamentary committee. I am very grateful for the work those people in my home province of British Columbia have put in on this bill and for their comments. I met with them, with some patients and with some people who were the main forensic unit is in my riding in British Columbia. It was very interesting. I was sitting across the table from two people who had committed murder when they were insane. They appeared to me from what I could see that they had made substantial progress on the road back to sanity.
These are very difficult cases. What do we do with these people? We have the notion of retribution from the public, we have the public interest, and on the other hand we have the human rights of these people. They should not be sitting locked up when they are basically cured. It is a very difficult issue. The bill attempts to deal with this.
Let me deal with some of the provisions of the bill. As I said, the Criminal Code provisions for the mentally disordered offender contain a lot of inconsistencies and omissions and often lack clarity. Much of the law dates back to 1892 or earlier. The law of insanity in Canada is really a 19th century law. The language used to describe mental disorder is archaic and in some cases the authority given to the courts and to the lieutenant- governor is inappropriate.
On May 2, 1991 the Supreme Court of Canada in the Swain case decided that one of the key provisions of the Criminal Code was contrary to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and therefore invalid. The court gave Parliament six months to clean up the law. This was extended and Parliament ultimately produced Bill C-30.

Back in 1976 the Law Reform Commission of Canada in its fifth report called Mental Disorder and the Criminal Process stated that major changes were required in the way the criminal law dealt with persons suffering from mental disorder.
The Department of Justice carried out additional studies to gather data on exactly how the existing system was operating. It also conducted extensive consultations with the federal and provincial government and produced a draft bill in 1986. We are just getting to that bill now.
This is a big bill. The thrust of these amendments is to modernize and streamline the law in response to demands for change by legal and medical practitioners and interested organizations in accordance with the government's 1990 undertaking to review federal legislation affecting the handicapped.
Amendments are based on the recognition of the complementary roles of the federal and provincial governments. We have two governments involved here. We set the law but basically the provincial governments look after health and the institutions and make a lot of the decisions: a typical Canadian way of doing things. Therefore we have to deal with the provincial governments as well.
I might add that I believe my friend, the member for Moncton, has introduced an amendment that there be a review of this bill. I think that is a good idea. We have been busy with gun law, young offenders, extradition and you name it in the justice area. I have a feeling that we should have given this bill a little bit more scrutiny. I think we have protected ourselves by this review. Where there is good will to make this work it will work. I think we are going to have to come back to the bill.
Let me go into a few more details of the bill. As I understand it, one of the first provisions is the idea of remand for assessment. I might say that I started my working career as a Crown attorney in Vancouver and was defence counsel there. I dealt on a daily basis with some of these remand cases, as crown counsels do.
A court may order that a person be sent for an assessment of his or her mental state. This is when a person is picked up for a criminal offence and is referred to as a remand. A person can also be committed under
Government Orders
the provincial Mental Health Act when a person is mentally ill. We are talking now about someone who is suspected of being mentally ill but is picked up in the system through a criminal offence. That criminal offence can range from shoplifting to assault to murder.
Currently the Criminal Code permits a remand only on the basis of medical evidence and only for the purpose of examination to determine fitness to stand trial. When the person is brought into court it has to be determined if he or she is fit to stand trial. The person is remanded, the case is adjourned, and the person is in custody.
The amendments will let the court decide the kind of evidence necessary to trigger a remand. The remand is expanded to include an assessment to determine the individual's mental status at the time of the offence, as well as to assist in making appropriate disposition or even a hospital order. This is good. This gives a lot more flexibility to the judge.
The traditional remand for fitness is maintained. Where appropriate, the court may order treatment with safeguards for the sole reason of making the accused fit to stand trial. It has to be determined right away if the accused person is fit to stand trail. This is to enable the person to have a trial as quickly as possible while witnesses are still available, before memories fade. We do not just want to lock the person away and not have the trial.
It is sort of like Alice in Wonderland. The queen said to Alice: "Off with her head and then we will have the trial". This time we are going to have a little fairer procedure. We will not take the head off before we have the trial and we will have a speedier trial.
There is provision for a five-day assessment. Normally when a a person came into court and we did not know whether the person was fit to stand trial, the person was remanded for 30 days automatically. That is a big deprivation of liberty. If it is a shoplifting offence the penalty would normally be maybe a suspended sentence or probation.
Under this bill, as I understand it, in order to save time and money and minimize interference with the liberty of the person, subject to the assessment the amendments stipulate that a remand for a fitness evaluation will be no

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
more than five days, excluding any travel time, unless the accused and the prosecutor agree to a longer period. That is definitely an improvement in the law.
A new area of the law deals with protected disclosures as it relates to evidence of statements made by the accused. Once we remand the accused for psychiatric assessment, the assessment is done by a psychiatrist or a psychologist. During that court remand period when the assessment is being done, there is going to be protection in the law so that what the accused says to the psychiatrist and the psychologist cannot be used as evidence in court without the consent of the accused. There are some exemptions to this rule. I will not go through the exemptions, but that is putting it simply. And that makes sense, does it not? We want the person to be able to unburden himself to the psychologist or psychiatrist to see whether that person is really fit to stand trial. That is an improvement.
The other area that the bill deals with is the verdict of insanity. Section 16 of the Criminal Code sets out the defence of insanity, and that is amended to modernize its terminology. I said that this insanity notion in our law goes back to the 19th century, to the 1892 Criminal Code, as a matter of fact. Anyway, it is amended to modernize its terminology to make it more consistent with current medical use and to remove a subsection that was found by the court to be unnecessary. The amendments do not attempt to alter the judicial interpretation of the insanity test itself.
We have sort of moved to modernize it, if I can put it that way, but not completely. As I understand it, in the legislative committee that studied this bill members heard from psychiatrists and psychologists. They asked the committee to modernize the law, whereas criminal lawyers do not quite agree on the same terms as the psychologists and psychiatrists. I point out to this House that we still have to approach this. We may still have to come back after a few years and actually deal with modernizing the modern law of insanity. But that is a big project.
Consultation press reports over the past few years show that the general public finds it difficult to understand the present verdict of not guilty on account of insanity when it is known that the accused committed the act. They say that if he committed the act, how can he
not be guilty? In addition, a number of psychiatrists suggest that the verdict of not guilty permits the accused to continue deluding himself or herself that he or she has done nothing wrong. They say this may interfere with the possibility of treatment, if the person does not think he or she has actually done anything wrong.
That is what the psychiatrists say. I received a letter from one of Canada's foremost criminal lawyers, my friend Clayton Ruby from Toronto. He wrote to me about these proposed insanity amendments, and I will just quote one of the paragraphs from his letter. He says: "I do not understand why we fled from the idea that insanity does not produce a true acquittal. I like the idea that it does. This document"-that is the bill-"abandons that idea and creates some new form of non-criminal responsibility. Indeed I do not even like abandoning the verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity. I think people understand it and I think it is a true acquittal". Well spoken, like a true defence lawyer.
We see the difference between the medical group and the defence lawyers. Parliament has to struggle to find an adequate definition. I am just telling the House that I do not think we have quite found it, but we are moving that way.
Some American states have moved to the verdict of guilty but insane. This runs counter to the basic principle of Canadian criminal law that to be convicted of a crime one has to do the act, which is called the actus reus in criminal law, and you have to have the mental state, which is called the mens rea in criminal law. You not only need the wrongful act; you need the guilty mind. If you are insane, how can you have a guilty mind? Therefore you are not guilty, if I can put it very simply. That is the Canadian law in two sentences with respect to insanity.
This bill therefore proposes a verdict here which declares that the accused committed the act or omission but is not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder. To me that sounds reasonable, but I do point out that criminal lawyers that know more about the law than I do, Clayton Ruby for example, say this is too much of a hybrid. We are going to need another look at this as we go on.

With respect to the disposition, once a finding of insanity or unfitness is made, the individual must be ordered by the court into strict custody until the pleasure of the lieutenant-governor is known. What a quaint phrase. The lieutenant-governor is the cabinet basically or the lieutenant-governor of the province acting on the provincial cabinet. You can be locked up and the key can be thrown away until the cabinet, politicians, let you out.
You may get someone who has killed a couple of people in his family because he is mentally insane or even someone who has done something not so serious. The lieutenant-governor is going to hesitate to sign that order and you are going to be locked up for a long time. Of course that is the problem.
Such persons are then held, as I said, in the psychiatric facility under the jurisdiction of the provincial lieutenant-governor. About 1,100 Canadians are now being held in custody in this fashion. It is important to recognize that none of them has been convicted of a crime. Indeed many of them have not even had the benefit of a trial to determine whether in fact they committed a crime. In many respects their situation is worse than if they had been convicted of the offence charged. Indeterminate custody under a warrant of the lieutenant-governor is at the lieutenant-governor's absolute discretion.
The Criminal Code provides for the creation of a board of review in each province but, as the parliamentary secretary said, for a while in the territories and British Columbia there was not even that board of review. The lieutenant-governor is not obliged to set up a board of this kind or to follow its advice. Board procedures are not set out and neither the decisions of the board nor those of the lieutenant-governor are subject to appeal.
We can see why the Supreme Court of Canada said that there were some very questionable procedures under this law from the point of view of the charter of rights.
Under this bill review boards become mandatory and will assume the decision-making role currently filled by the provincial lieutenant-governors with regard to persons found insane or unfit to stand trial. That is the most important part of the bill and the part I think all of us in this House support.
Government Orders
To assure that persons who are found unfit to stand trial and not criminally responsible because of mental disorder are dealt with expeditiously, the bill provides that the court can make a disposition if it is satisfied that it can do so readily and that a disposition should be made without delay. If the court does not make a disposition, the review board shall make one within 45 days, within a maximum of 90 days, if the court is satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist. The review board must review a disposition made by the court within 90 days of it being made.
That is what the bill sets out. It is technical but that is what the bill as I understand it sets out. We are going to see how this works. I know we have the pledge of the government that it will watch to see how this is going and review the matter if it is not working.
A guiding principle with regard to all decisions and dispositions under the proposed legislation is that the court or review board shall use the least intrusive or restrictive option consistent with the protection of society. For example, the court or review board might allow someone who committed a theft who is not dangerous and willing to submit to psychiatric treatment on a voluntary basis as an out patient to stay at home rather than occupy a costly hospital bed. Such a condition would be subject to supervision and so on.
I just want to make this point. This tendency to treat people with mental illness outside institutions is basically I think a good idea.
We have to accompany that by resources. We can enact all the laws we want here but if we do not provide resources and the provinces do not provide resources and the government does not provide resources, we cannot rely on charity. We need real resources to deal with these people. I think that is the mistake that has been and is being made.
There have to be professionals who can come to visit these people. There have to be good facilities and treatment centres and so on, and I think that is where we keep falling down. If we fall down, we are going to have a major problem in Canada like in other countries where we have a lot of people basically on the streets, homeless, with mental illness problems. We just do not want to go that route. I warn the government about that because we are on our way down that road.

I thank the House for its permission to conclude my remarks even though my time has expired. I just wanted to add that there is a provision for capping. There would be outer limits as to how long you can hold a mentally disordered accused. I think that is good. I think it is about time we had that, and I think that was what was said in the Swain decision.
As I understand it some provinces will have to amend their mental health legislation to bring it into line with the new Criminal Code provisions. I think my friend from Moncton did a good job in writing to the provincial people to get them to respond to this and to get them to know what is going on.
That means the capping provision of this bill will be delayed for some time. I know that is going to happen and I hope that will come in sooner rather than later.
When we review this again we should have a look at the protection of society with respect to dangerous offenders, which is covered by this matter. The dangerous offender provisions will be amended here in the bill consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. There will also be provisions for hospital orders, dual offender status and amendments to the Young Offenders Act.
Let me conclude by summarizing my thoughts, and I will do it simply. We passed a very big and very complicated bill. It deals with a matter that is very complicated. I tried to make it fairly simple in the sense that we have new remand provisions, new capping provisions, provisions for a new board of review, and we brought it into the Charter of Rights and Freedoms so that people have their rights. I hope we have the right balance between the protection of society and the rights of the individual. That is the key to good criminal law and good procedure.
We have to work with the provinces and we need to have some resources to deal with the people. We have to continue to consult people in the field.
Having said all that, and I thank the House for giving me a little extra time, on behalf of my party we would agree to this bill going through today. I know when it passes here it will go to the Senate and I expect it will be the law of Canada very shortly.
Again I would like to express the view that we will have a review of this bill in a few years and the provinces will act quickly and efficiently in getting their boards and facilities in order.

Mr. Speaker, we are losing the battle to the ugly multi-million dollar pornography empires. The government must address the increasing presence of pornography in our society. It is time for legislative action.
Pornography promotes the degradation and sexual subordination of women and children. It desensitizes its users to the pain of the women and children who are used to produce the pornography or who have to deal with the men who use it.
Pornography injures women and children. It injures them by its existence, its production and its use. Canadian women will not achieve equality until violent and degrading pornography no longer exists.
Appearing before the committee last year, the Minister of Justice said she was examining the pornography issue. I urge the government, in its fight to stop the violence and inequality with which women live, to introduce tough anti-pornography legislation now.

Mr. Speaker, recently Preston Manning stated: "Farmers must become accustomed to living with less and farmers must reduce their dependency on government subsidies".
This irresponsible statement shows that Preston Manning evidently lacks knowledge and understanding of the farming community. Does he know how much it costs to produce a bushel of wheat and what it sells for on the world market? Does he know that 80 per cent of what we produce we must sell on the world market?
Since 1985 our government has assisted the agricultural industry by providing $12.5 billion. We have brought in the GRIP and NISA programs. We continue to strive for the clarification and strengthening of article XI of the
GATT negotiations. We have always and will always continue to support our farmers.
To reduce the national debt is a laudable goal, one to which this government is committed. But we will not do it to the detriment of Canadian farmers.

Mr. Speaker, the outcome of the current Uruguay round of multilateral trade negotiations is of critical importance to Canada's egg, dairy and poultry producers.
Among agricultural producers in my riding and throughout Alberta there is widespread and strong support for the strengthening and clarification of article XI.
This section of GATT, as you know, allows for the establishment of import quotas to support supply management programs which have ensured fair prices to producers based on their cost of production. It has done so without subsidies and without dumping on international markets.
There is significant concern that despite our official commitment to article XI, Canadian negotiators will be pressured into accepting tariffication. This would result in insufficient protection.
To quote one of my constituents: "Tariffication is in direct contradiction to the use of supply management as a permanent means of ensuring that producers achieve adequate domestic prices based on their cost of production".
I ask members of the House to encourage Canadian negotiators at GATT to continue to stand firm in their commitment to article XI and to ensure my concerned constituents that they will not become sacrificial lambs in the process.

However, Canadian taxpayers are hoping that the government is doing something to get back the $4.2 million in interest-free loans it granted this company.
More than anyone else, I want to see economic development in the region of Cape Breton. However, one must question the government's intentions when it backs a speculative technologies company with shares that soared from 35 cents to $57 and then bails out of its own commitments.
Someone made a lot of money. Too bad it was not the Canadian taxpayer or the few innocent Cape Breton residents who had a short career with World Communication Network Investments in Cape Breton.

Mr. Speaker, this morning the Minister of Agriculture released details of the distribution of the additional $800 million in farm support and adjustment measures known as FSAM II.
Grain and oilseed producers will receive some $700 million of this in income assistance. On the prairies there will be recognition of eligible forage and summerfallow at a rate of 25 per cent of the payment on seeded acres.
I want to congratulate the minister for his understanding of the special conditions which prevail across the southern prairies, conditions which require summerfallow and which should encourage the seeding down to grass of marginal and erodible lands.
November 21, 1991

This assistance, combined with other payments and programs such as GRIP, NISA and FSAM-I, will put approximately $3.4 billion into the hands of grain and oilseed producers between now and June.
The average producer will receive total payments equivalent to about $40 per acre over and above his return from the marketplace in the next 12 months.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of my colleagues and particularly my colleague from York West.
As you know, across the country today tens of thousands of Canadians will be celebrating the 522nd anniversary of the birth of Guru Nanak, founder of the Sikh religion.
As Canadians are aware, the Sikh community within Canada has been a proud and vibrant one during the past 100 years, contributing to our nation's growth and strength.
In many temples today, Canadian Sikhs will be marking this day with special reverence. Canadians should be aware that Sikhism teaches compassion, tolerance and understanding of one another and, more important, that the human race is one as no distinction is made between colour, race, class or sex.
I am confident that all Canadians will want to join me on this day of recognition of the principle of respect for one another which was thought by Guru Nanak and which guides the lives of millions of individuals worldwide. The community's continued contribution to our nation's development is one which they may be proud of.

Mr. Speaker, the Quebec mining industry is looking forward to the signing of a new Canada-Quebec subsidiary agreement.
A new agreement is essential to help the mining industry carry out research on ore bearing deposits, mine wastes and exploration in the Abitibi-Temiscamingue and Chapais-Chibougamau areas.

Mr. Speaker, David Duke lost and lost badly to a discredited former governor who, except in Louisiana in 1991, would be without merit.
Edwards, the victor, sank into oblivion but David Duke is everywhere for he is now a presidential candidate. For whom? The media. Why? Precisely because David Duke, however marginal, is a racist and a Nazi and that, for the media, will sell newspapers, whatever the cost.
Enter the deputy Liberal leader. She knows the media. They will gather like flies around her if she can give them a Canadian Duke. Even if not quite, even though it may offend-

I know the hon. member feels very strongly about this matter, but I think that is getting very close to a personal attack. I know the hon. member would not want to do that. I would ask him to complete his statement.

Meanwhile, except for The Montreal Gazette, racism in the Public Service, a real Canadian issue, is absolutely ignored though raised in this place.
Do you want to know what is wrong with politics? Ask the media. They can be found in a herd.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Ottawa over 300 people gathered to remember a woman who was brutally murdered last week by a crossbow.
Patricia Allen's estranged husband has been charged with first degree murder in her death. Violence is inflicted against women most often by men they know. In 1989, 119 women were murdered by their spouses and that is 62 per cent.
As one woman commented yesterday: "We are safer on a dark street alone at night than we are in our homes".
Patricia's murder also shows us that violence against women cuts across the socio-economic spectrum. Violence touches or can touch every woman.

November 21, 1991
I am pleased to see recent initiatives by the justice minister which includes a commitment to incorporate a clear definition of consent in new sexual assault legislation, as well as her positive reaction to suggestions by my colleagues in this House that access to crossbows be restricted in law.
So far the government has taken small steps. I suggest now is the time to break into a dead run in the race to end violence against women.

Mr. Speaker, there is a growing personal financial emergency for many Canadian consumers.
There is now indication that many bankers are unwilling to extend credit so these consumers can consolidate their debts at lower rates. They are being forced to carry their debts on credit cards at rates of close to 20 per cent.
Others have been forced into the arms of a new breed of loan sharks, people who are demanding up-front fees for the service of making an application to a lender. Consumers are being ripped off by these sharks and there is apparently no legislation in place, federally or provincially, to stop the practice.
I am urging the government to consider forcing an end to this repugnant practice. I am equally urging that Canadian banks get off their assets and start working with consumers, providing them with the living capital they need.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, punitive lawsuits in the United States against airplane manufacturers have effectively shut down small plane manufacturing in that country.
This has resulted in a tremendous shortage of small planes world-wide. Canada is uniquely positioned to become the world manufacturing centre for small aircraft.
The Eaton group's interest in bringing Piper to Canada is an indication of this.
I urge this government to seize the opportunity to create thousands of new jobs by immediately making the development of a small plane manufacturing industry in Canada a priority by eliminating regulatory and legal impediments as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, for years aboriginal people in Canada have expressed concern about overcrowded living conditions and inadequate housing funding. On November 19, my colleague, the member for Prince Albert-Churchill River, asked the minister of Indian affairs to alleviate this overcrowding because without correction children in Indian communities will continue to fall ill.
The minister's response that existing housing programs were adequate ignores the many examples to the contrary. In my own constituency this week, a father at Canoe Lake, Saskatchewan has pulled his children out of school to protest overcrowding in his own home where his family of eight has been trying for five years to upgrade their living conditions. The Chief of the Canoe Lake Band says they have as many as 50 people on the waiting list for new housing.
Obviously, there are inadequacies in the aboriginal housing program that must be improved. I say to the minister today: look at the realities of reserve housing and increase the funds available to the bands to ensure that they have adequate resources to meet the housing needs of their members.

Mr. Speaker, the war in Croatia goes beyond the conceivable in this day and age. Croatians have been left alone to defend themselves against a Serbian dominated communist government and the fourth largest European army.
The Yugoslavian presidency has no control; the army is out of control.
In failing to recognize Croatia and Slovenia, the Canadian government is sending a clear message to Serbia and the Serb dominated Yugoslavian army that they may proceed with their slaughter without retaliation.
November 21, 1991

I call on the Secretary of State for External Affairs to recognize the legitimacy of the democratically elected countries of Croatia and Slovenia. Such a step would improve the desperate situation in these countries and help put an end to the brutal abuse of human rights.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday the government claimed that the Chamber of Commerce was a supporter of its economic policies. Today that same Chamber of Commerce rejected outright the government's economic direction.
This morning the Minister of Finance said: "Everything is going along tickety-boo except for two things. First, employment is going to go higher and second, no one has any confidence in the economy".
Has it occurred to the minister that if unemployment is up and no one has confidence in the economy that his policies could be wrong? How can he justify higher unemployment when 1.5 million Canadians are already out of work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are encouraged today by the September retail figures, which have risen by .8 of 1 per cent, which is a step and going in the right direction. Housing starts for the month of October were 202,000. There were 108,000 full-time jobs created in September and October. Interest rates are continuing to come down. They have come down by a further nine basis points. The bank rate today is 7.69 per cent. Those are all positive indicators.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce said today that the country is facing a national economic crisis, and it blames this government's monetary policies. Why does the
Oral Questions
minister refuse to change his policies, after predicting this morning, that unemployment, which already affects
1.5	million Canadians, will reach even higher levels? Why does he support a policy that maintains such high levels of unemployment and is breaking up Canadian families?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member in her busy schedule had a chance to read the letter that was sent to me by the Chamber of Commerce. As I interpret the letter, the issue that it is raising is the burden of debt both at the federal and the provincial level, the external debt level, and high interest rates. What it is really saying is that the government has to curtail spending.
I appeared before the finance committee this morning. I had recommendations from the New Democratic Party for further expenditures of $3 billion to $4 billion to kick start the economy. That would certainly run contrary to this.
As well, I think it should be pointed out that the debt to GDP ratio is going to stabilize in Canada in 1991-92 and then start coming down. The deficit to GDP ratio has come down by 50 per cent from 8.7 per cent to 4.6 per cent. That is by far a better record than that which has occurred in the United States. We are using its figures. It has reduced its deficit to GDP from 6.2 per cent to 5 per cent; we have reduced ours from 6.7 per cent to 3.7 per cent. I think that is a good record.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance himself this morning predicted an even higher unemployment rate. Has he been to the food banks? Has he listened to the unemployed who are losing hope across this country? Can he at least listen to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which has today issued a massive condemnation of his monetary policies? Will he please permit the Canadian dollar to come down to give hope to some Canadian families?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
I would be interested in knowing the hon. member's policy on the dollar. Does she want a fixed exchange rate? If she wants a fixed exchange rate, why does she not enunciate it in clear-cut terms?

November 21, 1991
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance. Earlier today the minister confessed, and I quote: "The unemployment rate in late 1991 and into 1992 will be somewhat higher than we anticipated". Somewhat higher than we anticipated? Mr. Speaker, he is talking about unemployment rates above 10 per cent. That means that tens of thousands more people will lose their jobs due to the economic nightmare created by this government's policies, that goes on and on and on. I ask the minister: Why will he not recognize that his policies are a failure and announce new programs to create more jobs right now?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: I do not know what is bothering the hon. member. A frank exchange-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am being criticized for a frank exchange, laying down the facts as we see them. The fact of the matter is that unemployment will be higher than we had originally expected because of a number of factors. I outlined them this morning: the overhang of consumer debt, the poor position of the corporate balance sheets. The fact of the matter is that the U.S. recovery is not as robust as was originally expected. I repeat, the Chamber of Commerce can have its assessment of the economy. The Conference Board of Canada just this week predicted growth in 1992 of 4.3 per cent. The IMF, a respected international organization, expects that Canadian growth in 1992 will be 3.8 per cent. The OECD, another respected international organization, expects that growth in Canada will be 3.5 per cent. This represents the best growth rate of any industrialized country in the world.
If that is what is going to occur, and I have every confidence it will, there will be jobs created, there will be economic recovery, and there will be price stability. That is our goal.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance says I am bothered. He should be bothered too about the tens of thousands of people in addition to the 1.5 million already out of work who are losing their jobs due to this government's policies. I am bothered and he should be bothered too about the 6,500 people in Windsor and the 250,000 people in Toronto whose unemployment insurance benefits are running out
this month and next month. They are being forced on to the welfare lines by this minister.
The minister announced today that he has found money to help our farmers, and we are glad to see this. I ask the minister: Why will he not also announce today that he has found the money for new programs to create more jobs for those people who are now out of work, rather than put more people on to the welfare lines? Why can he not do that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course I am concerned and bothered by the unemployed. But I am also concerned and bothered by the massive burden of debt that we inherited from the mismanagement of his government that is putting a very severe restraint upon us.
That spin doesn't work any more. We're not buying it.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: They say they don't buy it. I want to tell my hon. friend across the way this government has not added one red cent to the burden of Canada's national debt. Two hundred and six billion dollars was inherited, $197 billion worth of compound interest. That is what has driven up the debt. That is what is making it so difficult for us to extricate ourselves from the difficult economic situation that we face.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Today the Minister of Finance told the Standing Committee on Finance that he will finally be taking some action on assistance to farmers, and we are pleased to see that.
What was quite interesting was that the minister said that some of the revenues from this would come from unpaid taxes by corporations, $2.6 billion in unpaid taxes by corporations. Week after week in this House my colleague from Nickel Belt has been pointing out to this government the number of corporations that pay no tax. Week after week I and my party have been pointing out the number of corporations that pay no tax. The response has always been from the former Minister of Finance that they have closed the loopholes; from the Minister of State for Finance that the corporate tax system is fair and simpler. But the minister today says that there is $2.6 billion in tax uncollected.
November 21, 1991

I ask the Minister of Finance: How can this system be so inefficient? How has he closed his eyes for so long to this unfair tax system and what is he going to do about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party approves of and concurs with what we are doing.

We would like to see, Mr. Speaker, the government do much more. The Minister of Finance and his government could have done well to listen to the Auditor General in 1990 who warned this government that by reducing the ability to collect taxes and enforcement it was in fact reducing revenues, and today we see that is what has happened. This government better gets its act in order.

Medicare has been cut, health care has been cut, education has been cut, and many social programs have been cut by this government. After all these cuts and after this deplorable waste, the government has discovered that corporations are not doing their share and that there is money out there that could be recovered.
Will the minister recover all the money our corporations owe Canadians and reinstate programs for the people of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue will be outlining in some detail the initiatives that will be taken in this regard. I am pleased that I have the support of the hon. member in stepping up the collection procedure. We hope we will continue to have her support in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, I must say to the Minister of Finance that it is not a question of having our support. It is a question of this government not listening. Now it is out consulting Canadians. Canadians want a say and we say what the minister has finally admitted today, that we have not had
Oral Questions
a fair tax system and it is about time this government recognized that.
The minister is very good at projecting what will happen. He is the future tense minister: what will happen? He admitted today that unemployment this winter will be higher than he said it would be, that the deficit will be higher than he said it would be, and that the minister who predicted an early recovery was wrong when he said that we have declining unemployment.
I want to ask the minister how Canadians can have faith in this minister's projections about the future when he will not recognize the problems of today and when all his projections have been wrong.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member does not have to take my word for it. She can phone up the International Monetary Fund, phone up the OECD, phone up the Conference Board of Canada, phone up other organizations that do objective analyses and objective assessments of this country.
It is all well and good for the hon. member to preach gloom and doom, but some positive signals did emerge today. Retail sales are up, not down. Since September and October, 108,000 full-time jobs have been created so that is a good signal. Interest rates are continuing to decline. Housing starts are up. It is not all positive but, comparing the extrication of this particular recovery as compared to 1981-82, we are doing fine.
There was a lot of conflicting data in the 1981-82 period. As a matter of fact, within a year there were two months of negative growth. So as you come out of a recession you will get this sort of volatility, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Today, 19 Haitians are occupying by force part of the embassy in Port-au-Prince. Could the Deputy Prime Minister report to the House on developments in Haiti and indicate what steps have been taken to regain

November 21, 1991
Oral Questions
control of the situation and guarantee the safety of Canadian personnel?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I would respond to that question.
As the hon. member is aware, the Prime Minister while in Paris recently invited President Aristide to come to Canada for further discussions on this issue. We want to ensure there is democratic government returned to Haiti.
With respect to the current situation of the 19 Haitians who are occupying the Canadian embassy, the latest information I have received is that they are in fact still there. Threats have been made to our Canadian personnel and obviously on that basis they will not be appropriate, persons to be considered for refugee status. Therefore we are encouraging them to leave the embassy. I can assure the hon. member that all our Canadian personnel are safe.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for the information. I hope she will clarify what appear to be quite confusing statements.
The Prime Minister, in Paris, said that these people occupying the embassy are not asking for political asylum. On the other hand, external affairs spokesmen here in Ottawa say they are in fact asking to become political refugees.
The Canadian people would like to know exactly what is taking place, what are the demands and how are we coping with them. Can the minister indicate the Canadian government's position with respect to accepting refugee demands from Haitians, or are we rejecting them outright as the American government now appears to be doing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to advise the member that in the particular situation of the 19 who are occupying the Canadian embassy, based on the information we have at this point and the behaviour, the threats that were made
at the Canadian embassy, they would not be considered for refugee status.
We of course are continuing generally in terms of accepting people who meet our criteria for refugee status, whether they are from Haiti or from other countries.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The government has known for some time about a proposed joint venture between McDonnell Douglas and the Government of Taiwan, a deal that would transfer 3,500 jobs from Canada to Taiwan.
What specific measures will the government announce today to keep these jobs in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no agreement between McDonnell Douglas and the Government of Taiwan in terms of exactly what would happen if they joined forces. I think it is a bit premature to try to answer this hypothetical question.

It is not hypothetical when 3,500 more jobs in the aerospace industry are on the line, Mr. Speaker.
Again my question is for the Minister of Finance. Governments around the world, and now Taiwan, have recognized the importance of government investment in aerospace, yet our minister for industry and our Prime Minister recently went begging to the European community to get its permission so that Canada could give away de Havilland to the French and Italian governments.
Is this piecemeal, systematic dismantling of Canada's aerospace industry just one more plank in this government's so-called prosperity agenda?

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows we have been involved in the discussions with respect to de Havilland right from the beginning. He also knows that the memorandum has just been signed between McDonnell Canada and the Government of Taiwan. He is speculating on an agreement that he knows nothing about. Neither do we.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who announced today that $400 million of the farm aid package will come from unspent gulf war funds, and the other $400 million will come from next year's budget by way of requiring corporations to remit half of any income taxes that were in dispute.
Why did he not require those same large corporations to remit all of the $2.6 billion of disputed funds instead? This would have raised enough funds to more than meet the required farm aid package of $1.3 billion instead of simply cutting it back to $800 million?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, very simply because some of these accounts are in dispute and it will require legislation.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. The government decided to penalize farmers who have seeded forage crops on good class 1 to 4 farmland by paying those acres one-quarter of what was paid to those same lands seeded to grains and oilseeds.
Has the government already abandoned its brief policy of diversification, sustainability and market responsiveness? What is the reason for signalling farmers to plant grains and oilseeds instead of forage crops?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member obviously did not understand what the announcement today involved. The announcement today involved the culmination of discussions with the third line of defence committee made up of industry, farmers and provincial representatives. They recommended that we pay on seeded acreage and pay 25 per cent on summerfallow and 25 per cent on forage.
The hon. member also forgets that one of the reasons I did not choose the option to just pay on seeded acres- that was another option I had from the third line of defence-was because this government in FSAM-1 put forward $50 million in the prairie region to promote forage production and $22 million in the rest of Canada to promote forage production, making a total of over $72 million in forage production.
Oral Questions
Is the hon. member saying that those who summerfallow and those who seed are not eligible but only those who are in a soil zone or in an area where forage production can take place should receive assistance from this government?

Mr. Speaker, on Monday this government announced that it would raise the employment tax collected through UI premiums to 7.2 per cent, a higher rate than even the GST. This tax hike will mean fewer new jobs and smaller pay cheques for the Canadian worker.
I would ask the Minister of Finance to admit that by taxing jobs his government will put even more Canadians out of work.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that question has been asked in the House before and it has been responded to by myself and by the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
There are three criteria that have to be followed: first, the financial integrity of the UI account; second, the impact that it will have upon the employees and the employers; and, third, the over-all impact it will have on the fiscal accounts of Canada. All of these things had to be taken into consideration.
There was a range between holding the premium at $2.80 which would have generated deficits of $4.6, $6.2 and $7.3 billion in later years or a modest increase to $3 or an increase to $3.20 which would have balanced the account much quicker.
We chose the tradeoff, recognizing that it was going to have an impact and recognizing that we needed to put the UI account on a sound financial footing.

Mr. Speaker, the minister is always asking where he can raise funds. Perhaps he should have charged a commission on the jobs his government shipped to the United States.

November 21, 1991
Oral Questions
What this government must find particularly attractive about raising its employment tax, for that is what it is, is the fact that it makes moderate wage earners pay more of the cost of the high unemployment caused by this minister and his colleagues.
I ask the minister if he finds it just to make ordinary wage earners pay so much of the social cost of the Tory economic decay.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a difficult issue. I wish the hon. member would understand that it is not a matter of just simply postponing the burdens of today on to future generations.
There is a time when we have to start paying our way. We cannot postpone it. We believe it is time to bite the bullet and to make sure that we can preserve the financial integrity of this account. To fail to do that would increase the burden of servicing the UI account with a decreasing amount of benefit occurring to the unemployed. Surely the hon. member would not want that to happen.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
The demand for the government to take action on credit card interest rates continues to grow. Just yesterday the Consumers Association of Canada said that if credit card interest rates did not drop substantially within the next 30 days it would support a legislative cap on interest rates.
My question to the minister is this: How many days have to pass, how many calls for action will it take and how many millions of dollars in excess interest charges will be sucked from consumers' wallets before he and his government do something about this very real problem?
The better answer, as the minister has said from time to time in this House, is for individuals to endeavour to pay their credit card bills on the due date.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance.
Last evening the Consumers Association also said that it believes that there is sufficient evidence of gouging and rate fixing on credit cards to warrant an investigation by the Competitions Bureau. This is a very, very serious allegation.
My question is this: Is the minister prepared to order a fast track investigation by the Competitions Bureau to ascertain whether or not the big banks have, indeed, been taking obscene windfall profits from the pockets of Canadian consumers? Yes or no, or are you just going to continue to allow it to go the way it has been?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows because he is a student of these matters, the Competitions Bureau is an arm's length organization. It is an organization which I am sure he would want to operate without interference or direction from the Government of Canada. It has its duty imposed upon it by statutes. It knows its duty and I am sure it will carry out its duty.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister and it concerns the 55 per cent to 60 per cent Canadian content target for the Hibernia project.
Canadian manufacturers are concerned that no Canadian preference will be given or can be given under the Hibernia guidelines.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, the question of putting a cap on interest rates does not really solve the problem.
The difficulty this presents is that the tendency would be then for interest rates to cluster around the cap mark.
I ask the minister if he will guarantee Canadian manufacturers that indeed the 55 per cent to 60 per cent Canadian content goal will be attained.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, officials from both the Canada and Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board believe that these figures cer-

November 21, 1991

tainly can be met and will be doing everything possible in the future to make certain that it will be fulfilled.

Mr. Speaker, from all reports from Canadian manufacturers that is not true.
The Canadian steel industry, taking a specific, is in a crisis and in need of profitable domestic orders. It was anticipated that these orders would come from Hibernia. The member would know that last week Algoma lost a critical steel plate order to a Belgium supplier.
We know we can be competitive in this product. It has been suggested that Europeans are dumping plate into Canada.
Will the minister ensure that Canadian steel interests are safeguarded so that Canadian producers get their fair share of any further steel contracts for Hibernia?

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, Algoma can certainly lay the dumping charge if it believes it is in place.
The information that I have been given is that we will be doing everything in our power to ensure that 55 per cent to 60 per cent Canadian content will be there.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs. After the Wells-Chretien show of mutual admiration in 1990, which disgusted all Quebecers, we were recently treated to a Chretien-Clark meeting of minds on the subject of the federal referendum. What excuse does the minister have for being in league with the Leader of the Opposition in another attempt to put Quebec in its place and sabotage the implementation of Bill 150?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not discuss with my hon. friend the
Oral Questions
so-called complicity of a member of this House with Mr. Chretien, in view of his own considerable experience in this area.
The proposal is one we made in the throne speech: to table in Parliament a bill that would allow the government, if necessary, to hold a national referendum. This is about our commitment to table referendum legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs knows perfectly well that yesterday in the National Assembly, the Quebec minister of justice, in fact the National Assembly, was unanimous in stating that the federal government had no business trying to hold a referendum or preventing Quebecers from choosing their own destiny.
1 have this question for the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs: How can he justify this attempt to pass legislation that would steamroll Quebec's plans, especially Bill 150?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this question, because I think it is very important for Quebecers to know all the facts so they will have a good understanding of the federal government's position. Our position is that we are going to table a bill that will allow us to hold a referendum. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment.
Last night's fire at a provincial chemical storage site in Grand Coulee, Saskatchewan once again demonstrated the vulnerability of Canadian communities to the hidden threat of environmental accidents.
Under the Environmental Protection Act, the minister has the authority to establish a national code of practice that would ensure safe storage of all such facilities across the land.
Why has the minister not done so? More important, why has the government not guaranteed the public's right to know of the toxic hazard that exists within neighbourhoods?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been made aware of this incident in Saskatchewan, as is the case for most people.
We have offered and Environment Canada is always ready to work in co-operation with the provincial authorities when these type of incidents occur.
I think the hon. member would recognize that when these incidents do happen it is the provincial government's primary responsibility to deal with them. Storage is their primary responsibility. In fact, I understand that the new Minister of the Environment from the Government of Saskatchewan has ordered an inquiry into this fire to determine why these substances were stored where they were.

Mr. Speaker, for the same minister.
There has been a number of these incidents across the country, to the point that it is now the responsibility of the federal Minister of the Environment.
Section 35 of the act, if indeed the minister has read the Environmental Protection Act, gives this minister the authority to make an interim order in respect of any toxic substance and to put in place whatever regulations are required.
Will the minister agree today to make such an order that is within his authority to ensure safe storage at all hazardous chemical sites in the country, and will he also commit to guarantee the public's right to know?
It is not fair to ask the Canadian public to live under the constant threat of a hidden toxic disaster.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:

In the area of the environment, the federal government's intention is not to be paternalistic. I know that there is some difference in the hon. member's approach to the federal government's role on the economy, for example. He seems to object strenuously to the federal government having any role that will go beyond what the constitutional framework is. In the area of the environment he seems to have a very different approach. He cannot have it both ways.
We work in co-operation with the provinces and in veiy close co-operation with the Canadian Council of Ministers. When there were problems, for example, with PCBs we worked with the provinces to identify sites. On those that came under federal responsibility, we took action. On those that came under provincial responsibility, the provinces took action.
We intend to work in the same co-operative spirit in the years to come.

I have satisfied myself' through direct personal communication with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the November 19, 1991 statement to this House by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs is false.
I endeavoured to obtain a satisfactory resolution to this in writing from the government and to date this has simply been without satisfactory result. I believe this to be substantially beyond a dispute as to the allegation of fact because the statement made by the parliamentary secretary is the following, and I quote:
It is not only U.S. subs that have gone through there, but other
NATO subs have been there.

and let the member know.

Indeed there were transits through the Dixon Entrance in 1989
and 1990.
I do not think it should be necessary, once a parliamentary secretary or a minister knows that a statement they have made is false, for a member to be forced to come back every time in Question Period to get it remedied.

We now have an allegation by the parliamentary secretary who has access to information that members do not have from External Affairs and has stated on the floor of this House that subs other than U.S. subs have been using Dixon Entrance.
