speechtext: I am still enthusiastic about taking those documents up. I am sorry to hear they have not been tabled. I will endeavour to have them tabled tomorrow.

As chairman of the House of Commons Board of Internal Economy I have the pleasure today of tabling, in both official languages, a report on the
recently completed audit of the House of Commons administration carried out by the Auditor General of Canada.
On behalf of the board I would like to thank the Auditor General and his staff for a thorough and constructive review, the first comprehensive audit of the administration since 1980.
The report concludes that substantial progress has been made since 1980 and that the opportunity for further improvement is available in a number of areas.
According to the report: "Our observations do not suggest serious widespread problems".

The board was pleased to note the Auditor General's praise for dramatic improvement in the way public funds are used at the House of Commons.
At the same time, we are indebted to the Auditor General for his useful diagnosis of administrative practices needing improvement and his prescriptions for change.
To facilitate follow-up the Board of Internal Economy has created a subcommittee for audit implementation. This subcommittee will oversee the practical application of the Auditor General's advice.
All members of the House of Commons have an obligation to make the best possible use of resources provided by the Canadian public. The board will continue to help ensure that the recommendations which achieve that goal are implemented.

More specifically, acting on the Auditor General's recommendation, the board intends to strengthen the management of House-wide issues by re-examining and improving its information planning and decision-making systems. A review of the organizational and authority structure of the two management committees of the House administration and their relationship to the board has already begun. A formal program evaluation and internal audit function have also been established.
The audit report has concluded that the efficiency of administrative services varies. Measures are always under way to adopt best practices of well performing units in other areas which could benefit from them. Steps will
November 21, 1991

also be taken to improve the efficiency of operations and management practices where needed.
With regard to recommendations dealing with security, action will be taken to improve further the effectiveness of the operations of the service. As to the recommendation for a joint security force with the Senate, the board has noted that the Auditor General is currently conducting a broad review of this and other potential joint services on the Hill. The board wants to review the results of this study before reaching a decision on this matter.

On the question of making more information about House activities and members' expenditures public, the board agrees that budget documents should be made more readily available to the public.
The board will also undertake a review of the various expenditure categories which are not now part of but could qualify for inclusion in the members' operating budget.

In conclusion, the board was pleased to note that for almost all services more than 90 per cent of members who responded to an audit questionnaire said that then-needs were well or very well met. As a result the Auditor General concluded that:
Clearly managers and staff of the House have reason to be proud
of this accomplishment.
The board would like therefore to acknowledge the hard work and dedication of all House employees and express to them the board's appreciation for the high standard of services they have rendered to the House and the public of Canada.

The House resumed from Friday, October 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andre (p. 4030), the
Government Orders
amendment of Mr. Dingwall (p. 3887) and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Riis (p. 3881).

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to have the opportunity to enter this debate on decorum in the House of Commons, which was a motion prompted by some unfortunate events in the life of the House recently, the nature of which was not reflected in the government's motion.
What prompted this motion in the first place on the part of the government was a need to respond to the public perception that life in the House of Commons was deteriorating and what prompted that perception of deterioration was the use of racist and sexist language.
Yet the motion we have before us from the government talks about general matters of decorum and fails to make the appropriate distinction between general matters of decorum and the use of racist and sexist language. I think that is, if I understand the amendment from the Official Opposition, what the amendment seeks to do. It seeks to make it clear that it is a distinction which needs to be made by the government and by the motion so that the government is not able to buiy the embarrassment which it quite rightly should feel about the behaviour of the members who used the racist and sexist language in question in the larger issue which has existed for some time of House decorum.
Our amendment has to do with the question of political parties taking responsibility for the behaviour of their own members. Therefore it points to the need for the government to respond rather than just simply asking the House to respond to a situation in which certain behaviours or the use of certain language by members might call into question whether they should continue in their particular parliamentary duties. This is an issue the government has not been willing to face up to and which our amendment tries to address.
I might also say a curious thing happened with respect to this motion. The government House leader said there was going to be a free vote on this decorum motion. I am not sure why he felt this was important. I do not know whether he has people in his own caucus who want to vote against the decorum motion and is freeing them up to do so. What could he possibly have meant by declaring a free vote on a motion which encourages good decorum in the House of Commons? Is there dissent, debate and

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
discussion within the government caucus about whether decorum is a good thing in the House of Commons?
If it is a free vote then why is the House leader, after having introduced the motion, speaking on behalf of the government as to the acceptability of certain amendments? If it is a free vote then it seems to me that the government House leader cannot negotiate on behalf of that collectively known as the government caucus as to whether the NDP amendment or the Liberal amendment is acceptable. Therefore one can only speculate as to what goes on in the dark recesses of the government House leader's mind as to what constitutes a free vote. First, although I am certainly not against it in principle, why was this declared to be a free vote in the first place? Second, why, if it is a free vote, does the government continue to negotiate in a way that is reminiscent of non-free votes, of more traditional party votes?
What I want to suggest today in speaking about the matter of decorum is that in spite of the need to address some of the things that have happened here in the last little while, the fact of the matter is that the incidents which became notable were incidents having to do with things that members said which they did not intend to be on the record. I think it would be a mistake on our part if we became preoccupied only with those things which have been said which people had not intended to be on the record.
The fact of the matter is that this place is as much in danger of being undermined by the things that are said on the record.
In this respect I am talking about the general matter of decorum, how members conduct themselves in the House, the way in which we ask questions, the way in which they are answered and the general way in which business of the House is conducted.
Much of what is said on the record and which is within the rules has contributed in the last little while to a general deterioration in the perception by the public of the House of Commons. I enter this one caveat and that is it is not the first time the House of Commons has been held in disrepute.
I can remember when I was a kid during the Diefen-baker-Pearson era, the Munsinger crisis, the Rivard scandal and everything else, when people thought that
political life in Canada would never recover from that all-time low, that muck-raking and everything that was going on, and yet it did.
There may be a certain extent to which political life goes in cycles and is renewed from time to time. We I think rightly perceive that almost all Canadians with the exception perhaps of that very strange 16 or 17 per cent who support the Conservatives would feel that a renewal is in order. We may disagree among each other as to what shape and what context that renewal should take, but I think there is almost unanimity within the Canadian public that renewal is now in order.
I do think that we have come upon a new time in the life of Parliament and that we may actually be in something which is not just cyclical but historically new and historically problematic in a way that other times of cynicism about Parliament and politics have not been. I think that has to do with two things that are related.
It has to do with the absence of real power on the part of members of Parliament and the subsequent substitution of the rewards of power and real influence, however limited that might be, on the part of members of Parliament and the subsequent substitution of publicity as that which has taken the place of whatever power members of Parliament may have had in the past and have subsequently lost.
I am not trying to do kind of a golden age thing about a time when members of Parliament had all kinds of power. Members of Parliament have probably always had to struggle to have as much influence as they could over cabinet, over the Prime Minister and over various other forces in our political process. The fact is, and I certainly feel this is the case, that since I arrived here in 1979 the power of individual members of Parliament and of members of Parliament collectively, whether expressed in the form of opposition parties or in committees or whatever, have been reduced.
I know that goes against the conventional wisdom on the government side, that as a result of the McGrath reforms the power of the private member, the individual member, has been increased and I want to go into that. I think that at some levels, in some procedures and in some ways that is true, but when we get to the fundamentals, when we get to things that really count, the power of Parliament, as Parliament or expressed through opposition parties or expressed through the decisions of

committees, has actually been reduced since 1984 rather than increased.
For instance, committees have the power to study what they want to study now instead of waiting for a government reference, the way it was when I first arrived here. The committees do not yet have the power to have their conclusions, after they launch these independent studies, respected by the government.
We have seen a decline in the enthusiasm people had for reform of the committees. As a result of the absence of a government prepared to respect the decisions, in some cases unanimous, of committees there is a decline in the belief that committee reform is actually working because no real power has accrued to those committees as a result of reform.
That is just one example. There are others. For example, the most recent rule changes have severely curtailed the ability of the opposition to get in the way of the government and force it to come to terms with criticisms of its proposals or legislation. I know some people in the public might say: "That is precisely the problem. He is talking about getting in the way of the government".
In many ways that is what this place is for. We are here to hold the government accountable, to get in its way, to ensure that it does not always get its way. We are here to represent alternative points of view and alternative ways of solving the problems the government seeks to solve with its legislation.
Over the years the power of the opposition to make the government listen, by making life difficult for it, has been eroded. This ability to delay things ought not to be regarded in the entirely negative way that it is sometimes regarded. It seems to me that the notion of delay has been unduly discredited. What we try to do here, especially when the government is trying to do something that we think the public is dimly aware of or does not realize the full consequences of, is hold things up until public opinion can be informed or mobilized, depending on the particular view of the public.
There is always a political judgment to be made by the government and the opposition. When we hold things up we might pay a political price if we are wrong in our political judgment. We might be seen as holding something up that in the final analysis the public thinks is
Government Orders
good, or at least all right. The government has to make that same kind of judgment. However, lately the rules have become so skewed that we rarely have to make that judgment any more because we cannot hold up anything long enough to feel that we are in a position requiring us to make that judgment.
In the absence of that kind of power there is a tendency on the part of members of Parliament to want their constituents to at least know that they are here. How do you do that? You show up in the media. You have to be seen, not just on the parliamentary channel but on the news if you can manage it.
In the absence of this real power, which can be respected and used, members of Parliament are behaving irrationally for very rational reasons. In order for people to have the impression that they are doing something when the things they used to be able to do they are not as able to do as a result of changes in the rules or because changes have not been accompanied by the appropriate attitude on the part of the government to give those reforms real substance rather than just procedural reality.
The wrong kind of behaviour is rewarded in this place by attention. People wonder why. I am trying to explain why I think it is so. Members who are unwilling to play this game are condemned to a life of relative obscurity. Members who are by nature unwilling or unable to play that kind of attention seeking game are condemned to a life of obscurity. They may tiy to find other ways to combat it politically, such as being good constituency members or utilizing other strategies for surviving that kind of obscurity.
The fact is that this is one of the central problems in the House of Commons today. Unless we address it, we are not going to get to the heart of that.
There is never going to be a relationship that is completely equal. The government is always going to hold the upper hand to some degree. That is as it should be. The government is the government.
However, when there is a completely lopsided arrangement like we have now it is no longer the negotiation of peers. It is simply the semblance of civility that exists when you are in a room with a big bully known for

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
his violent behaviour. You try to get along because you know what happens if you do not get along.
That is the relationship we are in now. If the power relationship was more equal or more balanced then we would be able to do things that people are sending us here to do.
I will give a couple of examples. In recent weeks we have had back-to-work legislation a couple of times. As a result of the fact that back-to-work legislation is something the government tends to need that day and because this government has not yet figured out a way to streamline the rules in its own favour, there is still the odd occasion when it actually needs our help to get something through that same day.
When the government needs us-as it should; after all we are not just furniture around here-time and time again we are able to do constructive things.
We are able to work together. We are able to say to the Minister of Labour that if you want that back-to-work legislation concerning the grain handlers at Thunder Bay by such and such a time, maybe you had better listen to the grievances the union has and ensure that pensions are on the table.
It had to put pensions on the table, and that was a good thing. We all agreed upon that. It was a constructive event because the power relationship was the way it much more often used to be when the ministers had to depend on members to get their estimates and various other kinds of things through the House, when members of Parliament had real power over the government instead of just acting as a facade for the parliamentary dictatorship that is emerging.
It was the same with the back-to-work legislation on the postal strike. That was again a situation where there was a greater equality of power between the two sides of the House. We were able to say that it would be a lot easier and a lot fairer if some commitments were made to the workers with respect to the pay package that had been negotiated up to that point and if the imposition of arbitration was not something which would bring everything, including money matters, back to square one.
We were able to do that, although Canada Post has since tried to fudge on that commitment. That is another
example of what this Parliament can be like. I sometimes feel that in those few moments when we are doing things, where we are needed by the government, that is what Parliament ought to be.
When all of us are important and all our views are taken into account what comes out of the Chamber eventually reflects, in so far as is possible, the concerns of all the people in the Chamber. That is not always going to be possible.
I am not trying to be naive about this, but I use it as an example. If we could find a way to restore and enhance meaningful power on the part of members individually and collectively, a lot of the behaviour that we do not like would disappear.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was going to leave the Chamber when I heard the hon. member begin to speak.
I was very interested in what he had to say because he worked so hard on the McGrath commission that brought about the first big blush of parliamentary reform. I am pleased that he spoke. I heard some very useful thoughts and ideas.
I would like to respond to him. One night two weeks ago was not a very pleasant evening. He rose to try and get some information and the Speaker would not allow it to be put on the table at that point. We did have an early vote and it was really at the request of the member in private members' hour who moved the motion. The Whips were only vehicles to activate what the private member wanted, which was the subject matter to go to committee, no vote to be held, and it was blocked by a separatist in the Chamber.
So just to clear the background, I understand people did not understand that background in the heat of the moment. It really was what we had to do, if we were to respect private members' hour. We had to follow the wishes of the private members and that is how the Whips functioned on that evening.
I would also like to just say that it is a funny kind of a day. We had a few statements about decorum before we got into this and I was going to rise and decided not to and I went to the table afterward. We have a Standing Order 31 and there are rules related to that. It is the first part of the Question Period. Today we had 15 statements

made by 15 different members. Seven of them broke one rule, the length of time rule. Nobody called them to account. Will there be any punishment tomorrow because they took other members' time in the sense of them being ignored and not recognized? I personally think there must be. I think a rule without enforcement is worse than no rule at all. I think that is part of what has gone wrong.
I agree with the member totally that the wrong behaviour is rewarded in this place. If the refereeing was such that the wrong behaviour could not and did not occur then perhaps some responsible behaviour would be rewarded out of this place. When you give television a picture of somebody breaking the rules of the Chamber in terms of language or attitude versus a calm, rational statement, they will take that bad picture and put it on television 10 times out of 10. Unless this place stops it when it starts then that is the way the institution gets portrayed.
I back the member totally when he says that the wrong behaviour is rewarded and it should change. Wrong behaviour should be penalized and then ignored.
In my early days in this Chamber we were filibustering the Constitution. I raised a point of order for about an hour on what time it was and which clock was the right clock. I did not break a rule, but I did try and delay the government from doing what I thought was wrong. The Speaker was embarrassed because television used that argument of the clock with great repetition. I was not recognized for 33 consecutive Question Periods. After 31 I rose on a point of order and I was on the list, but the control is in the hands of the Chair, the referee. Nobody needs to be recognized ever in this Chamber. If we misbehave I suggest to the Chamber we should not be recognized for some suitable period of time. Then the reward, which the member is seeking, does not occur.
The use of inflammatory language, the use of personal insults, that kind of behaviour, which all of us abhor in our colleagues of all parties, will not be brought to a standstill until we cease to reward it. When you are a politician, being ignored, not being allowed to catch the camera and not being on television are the basic ways available to us to punish. But it has to emanate from the Chair. It simply has to emanate from those control
Government Orders
buttons that sit on the arms, that cut members off, that switch cameras.
I do not know whether the member would agree with me, maybe not totally, but does he and his party agree that the inappropriate behaviour that brings the institution itself into disrepute has to be brought to a halt? Then not only should we have equal powers but I think equal power comes from equal respect.
In this Chamber you get your way with your colleagues of all parties because they respect you. It has more to do with that I think when it comes to legislation and amendments and so on than anything else.
There are other games we get into from time to time. Over the years I have seen members of all parties who have had enormous influence on a variety of events simply on the basis of the homework they have done and the respect they have earned from their colleagues.
Inappropriate behaviour detracts from respect. Appropriate behaviour gives us respect.

Madam Speaker, I believe the hon. government Whip was referring to the vote which took place on the private member's bill of the member for Winnipeg-St. James which prompted the anger leading to the grabbing of the mace.
My understanding of it is different from my own conversations with the member for Winnipeg-St. James. When I talked to him at that time I certainly was not under the impression that he had requested the early vote. He seemed as surprised by it as anyone else. I understand that there was a move to refer the subject matter to committee and not have a vote. All that happened with the consent of the member.
The vote had finally been caused because of the refusal of the Bloc Quebecois to give unanimous consent for it to be referred to committee. The decision to have the actual vote after a four or five minute bell was something decided by the government Whip and the opposition Whip. It certainly made a lot of members very unhappy who, myself included, were on their way to the Chamber to vote for that private member's bill.
I think it does raise a question. I am not sure what the answer is. I am not suggesting that the answer to the question of the role of government Whips in the deter-

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
mination of votes for Private Members' Business is easy. There could conceivably be-, I am not saying this happened on this occasion; the government and opposition Whips may have had good reasons in their own minds-collaboration on the part of the two Whips against a member whose motion was coming up for debate and was not well liked. An early vote might work against the possibility of it passing.
I think that is a concern. Possibly we can address that in the Standing Committee on House Management in the long list of concerns we must consider.
As for the hon. member's comments about the Chair I have to say with greatest respect to the Chair that I think there is a great deal of truth in this. I have said this before. When I first arrived here in 1979, if the Speaker thought that your first question had been too long or had been answered, you simply did not get recognized for a supplementary. It happened to me.
I would stand up and be standing there and somebody else would start talking. The Speaker used that power to discipline people. If you did not do things right you soon knew about it. How did you know about it? You knew about it because you did not receive a supplementary or did not get recognized, et cetera.
I know the argument of the Chair is that now that the party lists go to the Chair, the Chair does not have any recourse. We had party lists then so I do not think that fully meets the objections. One of the objectives of the McGrath committee report suggestion to have the Speaker elected by the whole House by secret ballot was to give the Speaker a greater not a lesser mandate to deal with the House on behalf of the House.
I know what the Speaker has to say about this. However, with the greatest of respect I think the Chair already has that authority. If it was used fairly a great wave of relief would sweep over the Chamber. I only hope that will happen at some point.
Finally with regard to the point made about respect versus power, I think the hon. member is right. Respect has a lot to do with it but it is also a question of power.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very happy to speak today on this motion of the government. I certainly agree that it is something this House has to address. It is something that each and every one of us has to think about very seriously.
I was once a student in a private boarding school. The sisters there used to give lessons in savoir-vivre. That is how to behave, how to treat your fellow classmates, how to stand properly and how to address someone else. Many of us here could benefit from that kind of lesson and of being reminded many times that respect begins with respecting one another. It is an extremely important issue.
This is not a school. In essence this is the highest court of the land. It is the place where the laws that govern all the people of Canada are made.
Part of the reason for the lack of decorum in the House of Commons is the frustration of Canadians, which is reflected by and large in members of Parliament. There is a feeling across Canada-we are all very much aware of it-that Parliament is not listening to the ordinary Canadian. That is reflected here because often as members of Parliament we feel that we are not listened to. We feel that the government sets the agenda behind closed doors, comes out with a bill process, and often imposes that process on the rest of the members of this House, including the backbenchers on the government side. It is extremely frustrating. We have been elected to represent the people in our ridings, yet it is almost as if we are not allowed to completely do our job when this process is under way.
First and foremost we must open the process up. Perhaps we need more pre-study of bills, more open discussion, and more respect for each other's opinions. We will not always have the same opinions. We do have a parliamentary democracy. A parliamentary democracy is made up of different parties. Different parties have different philosophies, different rules, different things they care about, and different ways of looking at things. One is not any better or worse than the other, although we may sometimes believe that we have the answers. There will be some very strong disagreements on some issues.
I honestly believe that we can do this if we work together. I have seen some of these things work and work well when the government is open to bringing forward the best piece of legislation possible.
When I was on the finance committee I had the good fortune of working on a piece of legislation concerning which we were told: "We want you to come up with the best piece of legislation that you can". The government had brought forward some legislation and realized that it
November 21, 1991

was not the best it could be. It was a very difficult issue. What we came out with was certainly not perfect. However all parties worked on it together. It felt good to think that we could work constructively. We could support the bill because we knew what had gone into the bill. We knew its weaknesses and we knew its strengths. We were happy to do it. That is not to say that there were not reservations about that particular bill.
I would like to see much more of that happening.
When we talk about decorum in the House of Commons it is often in reference to Question Period. I have been a member of this House of Commons for three years now. It is not always easy, especially as a new member, to stand in this House of Commons and ask a question during Question Period. There are many times when you stand to ask a question in Question Period and are laughed at. There are a lot of comments being made. It is not an easy thing. I understand one of the reasons the government members sometimes do this is because it is very uncomfortable to have some of these questions asked.
I respect that the questions are uncomfortable, but I believe that Question Period is the only time and the only area right now within our Parliament where the government can be taken to account and can be questioned on some of the things it has done.
The government Whip spoke a short time ago and said: "Well, you know we have to enforce times and the Speaker has to be more strict and he has to turn the button off and not recognize people". The problem with that is it puts all the burden on the shoulders of the Speaker. I would hope that the Speaker can temper some of these limits with a little bit of mercy.
There are times when you stand up in the House of Commons and you are nervous. You may stumble on your words and it may take you a little bit longer than other times. I would hope that there is some mercy in this House of Commons, instead of automatically turning the button off after 30 seconds, because somewhere, somehow in some book it is written that your speech should only be 30 seconds long. There are some questions that are impossible to ask in 30 seconds.
Government Orders
I know we strive very much to have our questions within a certain limited time. I know the government also wants its ministers to answer in as succinct a pattern as possible.
Let us go back to Question Period and the fact that Canadians often only see the theatrics of Question Period, because that is the 30 or 10 second clip. That is not going to change very much. Television is here to stay. It is not going to go away. People like that. Much as we sometimes decry the theatrics, they will continue. People will continue to demand them and as long as we are providing the theatrics, television will show them.
The biggest thing we can offer is that we do not fall into the same traps. If we respond in a calm and professional manner, then perhaps there will be a balance and we will not only see the theatrics.
We live in a very fast changing world. You never know from one minute to the next what will happen and you have to be prepared for everything.
The other aspect is the televising of the debate. Did the respect of Canadians for Parliament go down after we started televising Question Period and the debates, or was it going to happen anyway? I would suggest that it would probably have happened at any rate.
If you go back over the history of Parliament, you find in many of the old debates that the same questions of respect for Parliament by the people of Canada have come up time and again. The same things are happening in countries around the world. Whether it is just television causing it or not, I would venture to say it is not. I would venture to say that it is happening around the world, not just in our country. We are not alone in having these particular problems.
I would like to remind the people of the House of Commons that I believe that television has actually brought more decorum to the House of Commons than there was before televising.
I was a student at Ottawa University 30 years ago. I thought it was great fun to come up into the gallery and watch the House of Commons. I can tell you that what I see today is far tamer than what went on in this House of Commons during debates and Question Period 30 years ago. It is a much calmer place. It is not half as noisy.

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
I can tell you that there was paper throwing, there was banging on the tops of the desks, and there were all kinds of goings-on. Of course it was not televised and it was quite pleasant as a student to sit upstairs and look down in here and make fun of some of the players and admire some of the others. Because I had the opportunity to visit this Chamber that many years ago, I am quite happy to report that it is a far different place nowadays than it was then, some of it for the better.
We talk about responsibility. I think everyone has to take responsibility. Parties have to generally just speak to their members and remind them of their responsibilities as parliamentarians to the people in their ridings.
I would like to believe that we will all take responsibility and not put all of the burden on one person who happens to be sitting in your place, Mr. Speaker. I think your position is quite difficult in that you must always be the person doling out the times and then, perhaps, the punishments. I do not believe it should solely be the responsibility of the Speaker.
We talk about responsibility. You know, when others show responsibility toward you, it is a lot easier in turn to show responsibility toward them. I will give an example. Ministers of the Crown are always going to my riding of Sudbury and making announcements on all kinds of things that I am not notified of. I have no idea of what they are doing in my riding, ever. I find out afterward when I read the newspapers.
I think that as a sign of respect it might be nice if we were told in advance, although perhaps not too far in advance because they would worry that we might say something. However, if we were at least warned that they were going to be in the riding, and perhaps invited to attend occasionally, it would make us feel more a part of what is happening with this government and it would make us feel better. Perhaps we would treat the ministers better as a result of this. It is a simple courtesy, I would think. Many times we probably would not be able to be there because they would travel to the riding when we were here in Ottawa, or something of that sort. But simple courtesies make you feel better about many things that go on in this House.
I would suggest that has to start happening, along with a whole new way of coming forward with bills and budgets. The government goes behind closed doors and
consults with the private sector or whomever it consults with. It then comes up with a budget which of course we are expected to answer to on the first day.
Of course that becomes a very controversial time. I believe if we could sit down in advance and perhaps lay out what we are facing and arrive at some decisions or at least be privy to some of the decisions, all Canadians would be better served. There would be less animosity derived from hearing that the government has to cut this program and we that program.
If Canadians were aware of all of the alternatives that had been considered during the process and exactly why these things had to be done, regardless of whether you liked doing them or not, it would make this a more humane House and a more humane process.
I was once on municipal council and I know this is very different from that because this is a party based house and municipal council was not. But it was far easier to strike a budget when the people of the area had followed through all of the deliberations and all of the difficult choices that had to be made. There was more respect at that point for the members of council who had to make those hard decisions. Sometimes there was animosity toward some of them, but it was a more open process and therefore it was easier to accept some of the difficult things. I believe we can move in that way.
I believe, though, that when there are some serious breaches, such as some of these sexist remarks and racist remarks, they warrant a serious reprimand.
I was at home when a member challenged the mace, and I understood why they reprimanded this particular member of Parliament, but what I did not understand was the severity of that reprimand versus what happened following the sexist and racist remarks. We have to somehow bring back a certain amount of equilibrium between the two, and I think everyone realizes that. I am hoping that this debate will actually change it.
We then talk about freer votes. I believe in freer votes.
I have absolutely no problems with free votes. I have certain principles and I would hope that at any time when I am asked to vote on things that would compromise my principles I will continue to vote against those things. I have no problems with that. I think the mechanism for freer votes is already in place, as my
November 21, 1991

colleague mentioned earlier, and it should be used more often. There are many, many bills that come forward in this House not based solely on ideology. There are things that we can all more or less agree on, things that some of us may disagree on but they cross all party lines. I think it is very important at that time that we be given the right to do what is right and to vote the way the people in our ridings would want us to vote.
It is not always easy to know what the majority of the people in the riding want. Often there are a number of very vocal constituents who will bend your ear, but they do not necessarily always represent the majority of the people in your riding. You have to use your own judgment many a time to find a way of determining what the rest of the people who are not speaking out really feel on an issue. That is somewhat difficult, and it has to do with each and every member of Parliament. Obviously during an election campaign people in the ridings must make sure they question the candidates to know what their feelings are and what their beliefs are, because then they can make some judgment as to whether they want to be represented by that person.
I am also very interested in the emergency debate questions. We had a debate on Croatia and Yugoslavia and the emergency there. I wonder why it took so long before we could have the debate on that question. The situation got progressively worse and worse, and I know that demands were put for an emergency debate perhaps as long as two months before the debate actually occurred. You wonder, as you sit here as a member of Parliament, why consideration was not given sooner to the debate. It is a simple question.
I am not too sure how the decisions are arrived at concerning emergency debates. I would appreciate if anyone later on can tell me how these things come about, whether there has to be a total consensus or whether something that is of vital importance to a certain large sector of your country should be considered automatically. I believe that in the past it was far easier for a member of Parliament from any side to rise and ask for leave to have an emergency debate on an issue of importance.
I thank you very much, Madam Speaker, for telling me that I am running out of time. I would just like to remind everyone that we are here to govern Canadians and we
Government Orders
are here because we are Canadians, and we are here to work for Canadians and for our country.

Madam Speaker,
I really did appreciate the speech by the hon. member for Sudbury. I think she expresses her feelings and her observations of this House and how it works.
I would like to make a couple of comments. She talked about bills being put forward to the House and said: "How are they prepared? Where do they come from?" I had the pleasure and maybe the honour as well as the disappointment of sitting on the other side of the House with the government.
I can tell her that bills are not being discussed in the government caucus. The caucus is not consulted. The bills are being prepared by the department. The minister brings them and says: "I am going to have first reading of this bill on this date". Naturally you cannot change the principle of the bill once it has been read the first time.
There is a lot of frustration by members of Parliament on the government side because they have no input in the legislative process. The same thing happens when budgets are presented. They are being developed by the Minister of Finance, the deputy minister of finance, a couple of advisers and probably the Prime Minister who is advised what it is going to contain.
Even ministers do not know. It is budget secrecy. I will just give you an outline of what was happening when I was there. I said to the member for Etobicoke-Lake-shore who was Minister of Finance at that time: "Look, you are going to present a budget and you want us to sell that budget tomorrow. We do not know what this budget contains. We do not know whether we agree, whether the Canadian people are going to agree, but this is the way it works. Tomorrow, you get your kits. You go on the phone and you defend that budget".
One of the things that this budget contained was the reduction of old age pensions. Naturally, if they had consulted the members, the members would have told them: "Look, if you want to punish anybody, do not punish the people who have worked for this country".
This is the way things are happening and this is why there is a lot of frustration in Parliament. People are frustrated because really they do not have any input. They do not have input into legislation. They do not have

November 21, 1991
Government Orders
input in the direction that the government is going to move and so on and so forth.
This is why there is a lot of theatrics in Parliament. You have to show that you are important. When you stand up in Question Period you become aggressive. You are shouting. The louder you speak, the better you are going to be. If you do not have the proper answer from the other side the government, everybody laughs and everybody is happy.
The member for Sudbury said: "In this House, when you ask a question of the government, it is not always easy to put it in 30 seconds". Then you are going to have laughs, comments and if you are a first-time member you might be a little bit rattled. You say: "What am I doing? Am I doing something wrong? Why are they laughing? Is my shirt not properly buttoned up?", and so on and so forth.
There is no understanding of what is being asked. It is a serious matter: unemployment, high inflation, suffering. Those questions are being asked by the opposition.
It was asking today about a lot of bankruptcies. It was serious. People are losing their homes and businesses. We do not want a smart answer from the other side. We want reality. Everybody wants to address this problem, whether it is the opposition or even the government members, but they have no input.
The only thing they can do is laugh and make a joke out of a serious question.
If we do not have a fundamental change in this House I think it is going to be extremely difficult to make progress.
I see that the Speaker says that I am maybe too long in my comments. I am sorry, I will conclude.
The fact is that we need to have a fundamental change in this House. There should be more free votes, more respect for each other, and we should not go back to the school teacher mentality in which the Speaker is going to be the only person who is going to correct and punish. We are the highest court in the land and so we should not deal like that.
The Whip on the government side would like that because he has the school teacher type mentality.
I am going to conclude because my time has expired. I congratulate the member from Sudbury for an excellent speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I thank the member very much. His comments lead me to believe that it is a question by and large of control by a handful of people perhaps on the government side and a feeling of total helplessness by a large number of members which creates some of the lack of decorum in here.
I believe that we have to move forward with the new and forget about the old ways of doing things. We have done things in this House for many years in that way. The sooner we open up the process, we change the process, we look at really responding to the people of Canada and open up the control process so that everyone has somewhat of a voice in the process, everyone will be much happier and Canadians will perhaps feel that they have been better served.

I do not have a question, but I have two comments. There is somebody waiting to speak. I will not take up much time.
In commenting on the remarks made by the hon. member from Sudbury, I could not help but note that in the motion there is a statement that Canadians have expressed alarm at the excessive partisanship in the House of Commons. It talks about decorum and civility.
I think what concerns Canadians with respect to partisanship is that partisanship prevents matters from being resolved, prevents problems from being solved, prevents questions from being answered. It is that kind of partisanship that causes major difficulties. I can think of many areas in which if the members of the House could get together on an instant basis they could resolve problems.
I think of the Supreme Court of Canada decision-and I hope this is dear to the heart of the hon. member-in relation to the so-called rape shield law. The Supreme Court of Canada declared a provision of the Criminal Code providing the rape shield law invalid. I would not like to think there is one member of the House who is opposed to the rape shield law, and yet we sit here day after day powerless, apparently, to do anything about it. They enter political life with a lot of enthusiasm, although sometimes they are rather naive about what they are getting into. That being said, I can see why the government wanted to table this kind of motion in the House. The motion is an attempt to respond to one of the public's concerns, namely how to make this forum, this House of Commons, more representative of the interests of Canadians and a better reflection of what Canadians expect of their elected representatives.

When you think about it, it is quite true we have the parliaments we deserve because we elected them, we 27 million Canadians. In the few minutes I have left, I would like to concentrate on that particular subject: the independence of members in speaking to questions before the House, the way we vote, the way we speak, the way we take part in debate, both in committee and in the House.
Television changed a lot about the way we behave in the House, and I am no exception. In 1976, when television came to the House, the Speakers of the House who had got along pretty well so far, did not have a list of members for Question Period, for instance. They had no list for members' statements-at the time we called them S. O. 43s, and today S. O. 31s, I believe. There was no list of speakers, either. During Question Period, the Speaker obviously had to recognize the opposition leader but, after that, he had to use his own judgment when recognizing members.
If we look at the records and statistics we see that Mr. Lamoureux, who did not have a list, nevertheless managed to give the Official Opposition, the third party and government members their fair share of questions.
The question arises: Why, in 1976, did the Official Opposition which at the time was the Conservative Party, all of a sudden come up with this list? It was television that imposed this discipline, as it were. In 1976, television could not cope with 40 members rising at once. It was absolutely impossible logistically, mechanically and scientifically. In any case, as far as television was concerned, it was impossible to broadcast this way.
So the Official Opposition decided, for the sake of order, to suggest the Speaker have a list. At the time this contributed to a certain degree of order in our proceedings, but it also helped the Speaker set up a system. Today many members, and I am one of them, think the list is a bad thing. In fact the list of members we submit to the Speaker, both for the S. O. 31s and for Question Period, is not entirely what I would have liked to see in the way of discipline. I see the hon. member for
Saint-Denis signalling that he agrees with me on this point.
I say this because I am one of those members who are convinced that the Chair should and can use its own judgment to ensure that during Question Period, during members' statements and during debate, there is a certain fairness in the order in which it recognizes speakers or the people who ask questions.
I realize this is one more responsibility for the Speaker. I realize this is an additional burden, but I think backbenchers would feel they were being treated more fairly if we had that kind of system.
Of course party discipline is involved. The caucuses will say that it makes no sense. Today, Question Period is the big show; it is what television and the media watch almost exclusively. Now, at 4.30 p.m., there are probably very few journalists watching the House, but between two and three o'clock you can be sure that many do.
Personally I think that such a list does not make for order, because it frustrates some members who want to ask the government questions about their constituents' concerns. I do not say that it solves the problem, but looking at what has happened since Speaker Jerome agreed to this list in 1976 and 1977,1 say that it is not a great success. Let me explain why I believe the list is harmful.
If a member of this House takes too long to ask his question or if a member uses language that is not quite correct, that is sexist, racist or otherwise offensive, the Chair is obliged to take corrective action.
During debate, in Question Period, when members make statements under Standing Order 31, during debate on Private Members' Business or on a motion, the Chair can and I think should act immediately to correct the error, the infraction, if you will, because the Chair maintains order in the House. It must uphold order. But if the Chair does not act immediately, obviously we come back to what I heard another member say, that sometimes it pays to do foolish things in the House. Let us be honest. A member who uses language known to be most inappropriate is rewarded for reasons that I do not understand by the media who cover him or her, sometimes with national coverage.

Using bad language is rewarded. It is an absolutely ridiculous system. I think that we must stop rewarding offenders as we seem to do around here. There must be a limit.
Personally I think that the Speaker should have the power to immediately discipline members who are out of order.
The Standing Orders were changed somewhat, with McGrath in 1985, if I am not mistaken, and the Chair was allowed to exclude a member for a sitting of the House without having to ask members to vote on the matter, under the following Standing Order ll(l)(tz) that was adopted. I will read it, because it is important:
The Speaker shall be vested with the authority to maintain order by
naming individual Members for disregarding the authority of the
Chair and, without resort to motion, ordering their withdrawal for the
remainder of that sitting, notwithstanding Standing Order 15.
The Chair has the power to throw a member out for a sitting.
I think that the second option for the Chair, not under the Speaker's authority but under that of the House, would be to have the government House leader move a motion asking the House to throw out a member who uses bad language or misbehaves, makes racist or sexist remarks or acts in a way considered inappropriate for this parliamentary forum. This second option always involved a motion, usually moved by the government House leader, whereby a member was suspended for a certain period: one day, two days or more. If the motion is carried, it involves a heavier penalty since the suspension applies to sittings not only of the House but also of committees.
As a second option, the government House leader can act by moving a motion in the House. Then the House, not the Chair, decides whether to exclude a member for one, two, three or four days. That is not a burden for the Chair but rather an obligation for this House through the government House leader. Let us look now at what happens in other legislatures and take the mother country, for example.

How does it work in the British House of Commons? Here, if you are ejected from the House following a
Government Orders
motion, you are ejected for a period of one day, two days or three days from the House of Commons and its committees. In Britain you are ejected from the parlia-mentaiy precincts, the whole caboodle: your office, the House and committees. It means that you cannot operate as a member of Parliament with parliamentary expenditures and an office, et cetera. It means that you have to go to your hotel, rooming house, or apartment and operate from there for the period you have been ejected from the House of Commons.
In my view that is a very different way of operating from here. I think it is a better way. It would not give those of us in this House who use abusive language or behaviour any recompense if they abuse the order of the House. That would be a tougher penalty and would be a heck of a lot more efficient, as far as I can see.
Madam Speaker, I talked about why I think you as Speaker can and should operate to keep order in this place. I have talked about the obligation of the House itself to maintain the status of MPs as role models. Believe it or not, some people believe that members of Parliament should be role models, that they should be exemplary in their behaviour, their language and their work.
Most of us try to meet those high expectations. Some of us sometimes miss. I accept that because the society we represent is not perfect and we are a reflection of that society. I would hope that we are trying hard to correct that. If the motion of the government is to provide any hope, the government should look attentively at putting in place a few changes, not very big changes, in terms of protocol, behaviour, and how we act in this place.
For example, I was Whip for six or seven years of my Liberal colleagues. When I first occupied the position of chief opposition Whip the practice was that when the Whips came in for a vote, every member of the House of Commons would be in his or her place. The Whips walked in after the members were in their places and indicated to the Speaker that they were ready to vote.
Today, if you are a Whip, you have to be a football player or even better because it is a heck of a challenge to get from that door to the mace. Everybody is standing there talking. There is no order and no discipline. There

is little to give the impression that we are indeed disciplined and orderly.
Change the Whip.

We have changed the Whip and I do not see any difference. The member says to change the Whip. I do not think we have to change the Whips. They are doing their best. We have to change our behaviour in this place.
For example, when the Speaker stands everybody should sit down. When the Speaker stands to adjourn the House, we should wait until the mace and the authority of the House have walked out before we walk out. Madam Speaker, every time for the last three, four or five years that I have been in this place, people walk out before you have even had a chance to stand and take leave of the House.
I have a few other ideas that I would like to share with the House, but you are telling me that my time is up, Madam Speaker. In closing, I would say that most of us participating in this debate have the interests of Parliament at heart. It must be an orderly place and it must be a reflection of what Canadians expect, which is the best in all of us. I hope that we will seek that in the near future.

Madam Speaker, I must congratulate my colleague from Vanier. He is a very astute member of the House of Commons who has also shown a very high degree of leadership. Certainly if all members of Parliament followed the type of leadership he provides there would be no question of decorum in this House.
My observations are somewhat similar to those of the member for Vanier. A very large portion of the members of this House are hard working, dedicated to the principles of developing laws and dedicated to making this House a place that Canadians can respect. However that is not the case in every instance. I guess we all are a bit abashed when we realize it is not the case.
I would like to comment on another part of this picture. As a new member coming into the House of Commons I faced the free trade debate and had to speak on it. Believe me, I was as nervous as anyone could have been about speaking in the House of Commons for the first time. I recall being heckled. I think I can recall exactly the members who heckled me.
It is true that those members heckle many others. Not everyone in the House is doing this. It is a particular group of people. It is not one political party. Every political party has people who seem to get very emotionally involved and very concerned about issues. We must realize that the House of Commons is a partisan place. It is a place of adversarial concerns where people do get emotional over issues.
I represent a rural Canadian riding. Farming is a major issue and auto manufacturing has been a major issue. My riding has been through very difficult times. When we speak of the farming issue or the manufacturing issue I do get very concerned. I probably get a little more emotional about those issues than some other members in the House.
When you feel that your issues are not being heard clearly, when you feel that the points you are putting across are not being accepted, you may have a tendency to respond in a negative way. That is not necessarily the way it should be but it is the way it is. I will do my very best to represent the concerns of my constituents and make sure they are heard.
I believe that the House of Commons does bring out the worst in people because of the press, as my colleague pointed out very clearly. The one liners that people are looking for are often what brings this House to a level lower than we would like to see.
The 30-second television clip or the newspaper headline, or some other vehicle by which people hope to get national recognition, often brings this House to a lower level. It is unfortunate that occurs. Many people also question me about the fact that the Liberals are always negative about what the government puts forward.
The Liberals are negative because they are the Loyal Opposition. Part of the role of the opposition is to look at the problems in bills and deal with them.
As my colleague from Vanier mentioned, the problem is not every member of the House. It is only a number of members of the House. I would say a small number. I also point out that the press and the method by which it generates news stories may also be a negative factor. That is very unfortunate as well.

Madam Speaker, I thank the member for Essex-Kent for his comments.

I think we agree on most of the points this motion addresses. Like him, I think that the present rules and conventions we have in this House are sufficient. We do not have to reinvent the wheel. We do not have to reinvent the mousetrap.
If we applied the rules we have in a good manner, in an efficient manner, this House would be a lot better. If I have anything to add to the comments of my friend from Essex-Kent, it would be to repeat that Canadians receive a reflection of Canada from this House.
I for one believe that my country is not being reflected in a fair manner when these words or unparliamentary acts are being used by people. With the tools we have we can dispose of that, discipline people and make sure the discipline sticks. We have to stop giving people who have broken the rules more publicity, more attention than they actually deserve, and stop recompensing them. That must stop.

Madam Speaker, I listened as I always do to the comments made by my colleague and long-time friend. I would like him to elaborate on what he said because he did not have the time to address the issue which we discussed this morning in the House management committee, the issue of how to impress matters on members, without having to change the rules. With a basic education-and by basic education I do not necessarily mean a university degree-well bred people, my parents used to say, behave like well bred people. This is so elementary that I am surprised that I should be stating such an obvious fact.
When someone has a good education, he behaves accordingly. I understand that in the heat of our debates we sometimes say things which we often regret afterwards.
But I do not see why we should destroy a Parliament because of such things. I look at my friend and colleague. I prefer, as you know, Madam Speaker, to call members by their name even if I am told that it is against the rules, but Mr. Darling is our esteemed colleague.

Those who watch him debating know he has learned how to debate vigorously, passionately, but has never seen fit to be vulgar.

The hon. member from Ottawa-Vanier tells us that we are often a reflection of what is going on in the country. I would therefore think that this institution should not be destroyed because the behaviour of some of its members is more or less acceptable. He could remind us, and I wish he would, of what went on in this place between 1964 and 1968. I assure you, my dear colleagues, that what you see today pales in comparison. Therefore, we must give hope to Canadians who are watching us by telling them that not all is wrong with this institution. That is the message I will convey to the House when I take part in the debate. We must not destroy the institution because of improper language or behaviour on the part of certain members. I would like my colleague, who is familiar with this subject, to elaborate on that if he has the time.

Madam Speaker, in the few moments remaining I would like to express a few thoughts on the motion before the House.
I want to begin by focusing attention on the statement in the motion that the House recognizes it is a national forum for the consideration of issues and challenges facing all Canadians.
I think those words were chosen very carefully because it is important to point out to Canadians that the House of Commons is not necessarily a forum for resolving problems. The House of Commons does not have the ability to put forward its own initiatives designed to resolve the problems that face Canadians, particularly in these difficult economic times. What the House does is consider propositions that are put forward by the government. Government members for the most part support those propositions and opposition members almost entirely oppose those propositions.
Therefore it is important to recognize it is in that atmosphere that the debate takes place. We are here to discuss the issues. It is quite understandable that there is an adversarial process at work in the House of Commons as we examine the initiatives the government brings forward.
This motion, I think, seeks to examine whether there can be a greater degree of civility among members in that adversarial process. The members should recognize matters of decorum to the point that the adversarial process can be more effective and bring about an appropriate conclusion to the propositions brought before the House.
If the public would recognize that process, we would have a greater and better understanding of the work of the House of Commons.
I do not want to be seen as defending in any way, shape or form a lack of civility in the House of Commons which I am sure is of great concern to you, Madam Speaker, as you see it on a day-to-day basis.
I think it is also important to remind Canadians that the House of Commons is not a place of worship. It is not a church. It is not a church service. It is not like listening
to a minister or pastor or priest delivering a sermon. You do not object to the statements made in a church or in other forums, but you do have a right to object to statements made in the House of Commons. If sometimes members are too exuberant in their expression against those statements, it may cause difficulties but it does not subvert the system entirely.
I think what members have to do, myself included, is recognize the need for civility and respond to that concern.
I would like to address another point that is made very clear in the motion and that is the partisanship involved in the House of Commons. It is very difficult to turn back the hands of time on a matter like partisanship. I know as I grow older I am less inclined to be partisan, but then something happens that awakens my baser instincts and I rise to the bait and become partisan once again. I hope that I and other members can control that, but we cannot really apologize to the Canadian public for a degree of partisanship. It has been a part of our system literally for centuries, through the British system and for over a century in Canada.
We can resolve to do better on the issue of civility. We can recognize the common interests of all parliamentarians and just the brotherhood and sisterhood that ought to exist among us. On the issue of partisanship, we can blunt our attacks. We are members of political parties. We are obligated to support a common goal, but I think the motion has served a useful purpose in reminding us that this is a national forum for the debate and discussion of issues. There is an adversarial process, but that process can be dealt with in a civil way and with a lower degree of partisanship.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisibility of moving the Harper memorial statue from its present site on Wellington Street to a site on the grounds of Parliament Hill and that the said memorial be designated as a statue commemorating the valuable contribution to Canada made by employees of the federal government.
He said: Madam Speaker, I have the pleasure to present this motion for debate in the House today, hoping that it will be adopted later on. This motion, as you said so well, Madam Speaker, has two purposes: first, to move the Harper statue and, second, to recognize government employees' valuable contribution to the Canadian society.

First of all I would like to start off by speaking of the Harper memorial and what it means. The Harper memorial is a wonderful statue close to Parliament Hill. It is located on Wellington Street, almost directly in front of Centre Block. It was erected in honour of a young man, Albert Henry Harper, a young civil servant working in the Department of Labour who had been hired by the then Minister of Labour, William Lyon Mackenzie King, later the Prime Minister.
Private Members' Business
When Mr. Harper was working for the federal government, going back home one night he stopped and, as was customary then, had a walk beside the Ottawa River. There were young people skating on the Ottawa River. Unfortunately they fell through the ice and two of them were drowning. Young Mr. Harper attempted to rescue them unsuccessfully and died in the process.
The tale goes that within two or three days a large group of citizens of Ottawa gathered together to erect a statue in honour of this brave young man. It was perhaps an unusual thing because there have been many other acts of bravery in this country that had not been recognized, but for a whole variety of reasons the statue was erected in honour of Mr. Harper. The site was chosen by the then Prime Minister, Mackenzie King. They erected this statue in front of Centre Block, but outside the grounds of Parliament Hill.
If anyone says that the statue should not be moved, I say to them it has been moved twice already. It was immediately in front of Metcalfe Street. It was moved eastward a few feet. Then because the salt of buses and other commercial vehicles damaged it, it was moved again a few more feet, this time closer to the sidewalk.
The reason I want to move it is because it is a valuable historic monument and it is in the process of being destroyed, by the corrosion and salt of the road, and unlike 1916 or thereabouts we now have many large commercial vehicles which could overrun the curb and hit the statue and destroy it.
I want to move that statue inside the grounds to protect it.

Let me tell you why I would, at the same time, attach a plaque, if we agree, to the statue commemorating the valuable contribution made by Canadian civil servants.

It was only a few weeks ago that five brave Canadians on a civil mission yet working for the military crashed in northern Canada and lost their lives. Two of the five came from my constituency of Glengarry-Prescott- Russell: Captain Judy Trepanier of Cumberland and Warrant Officer Robert Grimsley of Limoges. Those are two examples of civil servants who lost their lives working for their country, not in war, but nevertheless they made an immense contribution.

November 21, 1991
Private Members' Business
We sometimes take for granted what civil servants do and the valuable contributions they give. We have had a recent row between the government and civil servants and I do not want to get into the debate right now as to who is right and who is wrong. I could but that is not necessary. It will not contribute toward this debate.
The point I want to make is that we will all recognize the tremendous and valued contribution of our civil servants. Recognizing that, I feel that we should offer a small token of appreciation.

A few weeks after being elected in 1984 when I arrived on Parliament Hill-I had already worked here as a civil servant during many years-I was given a guided tour on the Hill, and during that visit we stopped in front of a plaque. The plaque was located close to the entrance to the House, but it has been moved since. On the plaque one could read the name of a member who had died in the Parliament fire. I was told: "Here is Hon. Bowman Law's plaque, indicating that he died in the fire. With him died six employees". I asked the security guard who led the guided tour who were these employees, but he said he did not know. When I asked the question at the Library of Parliament, nobody knew the answer.
After searching for several months we were able to get the names of the six civil servants who, along with the member, died in the fire in the Parliament Buildings. They had been forgotten. They remained forgotten for a long time.
Later, on February 3,1988, the present Speaker of the House decided, after I suggested it in a motion to the House in 1985, to put up next to the one for the member, a plaque commemorating the six employees who died during the fire of February 3, 1916. I am grateful to the Speaker for this kind gesture. It was not very costly. Taxpayers did not have to dig very deep for that, but I think it means a great deal.
What I am asking today in the second half of my motion is much the same thing.

I am not asking that we denigrate the honour of Mr. Harper by attaching another plaque to his statue. What I am saying is that at the same time as we recognize him, we say: "You, Mr. Harper and many other civil servants have given a lot to your country. This little plaque recognizes that you have".
That is all I ask. I know that from time to time we are asked by officials within parties, particularly those in government, to read a text that others have prepared asking us not to support this or to support that. I say to my colleagues that this need not be partisan. We have plenty of opportunity to do that. We just finished 10 minutes ago debating a motion which refers to the fact that from time to time we are much more partisan that we need to be. What an irony it is that only a few moments later we are discussing something for which no partisanship is even required.
Few funds if any have to be spent. The statue has to be moved anyway; it will be destroyed if it stays where it is. I am just asking to put it inside the yard. A few hundred dollars could well buy the plaque necessary to recognize the value of our civil servants.
If I can repeat something I have said before in this House-I have been around here for many years, not all of them as an MP-members will know that I started my career in this place on October 25, 1966 as a busboy. I consider myself one of those civil servants, not one of those dead civil servants who should be recognized. I ask the House to recognize those people who have given of themselves for us. If the government says it cannot afford a couple of hundred dollars for the plaque, I am sure I could raise the necessary funds by rounding up a few civil servants who could contribute $1 each.

I ask my colleagues to support this motion which is, I believe, in the spirit of what we talked about this afternoon. I listened to the remarks made by the hon. members for Saint-Denis, for Halifax West and others. They spoke with great eloquence to the motion of the government House leader which basically says that we do not have to be partisan all the time, as we were told and as we thought we should be. In a few minutes we might have the opportunity to prove that all these fine words,
November 21, 1991

that fine motion we debated this afternoon , were not in vain.

I know the members are personally well intentioned. I ask but a small effort of their time to demonstrate it this afternoon.
