speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to say at the outset that I agree whole-heartedly with the principle expressed by the motion put forward by my friend, the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
The statue of Sir Galahad has charmed many visitors to the capital over the years. It is true that salt spread on the streets harmed the statue and caused some problems with the present location so it was moved a little bit further back off the street. Everyone is now familiar with Henry Albert Harper's gallant and selfless act. It is well known to all of us here and all visitors who came. Most of us can look upon it and identify with it even in the present turmoil of the world. There is a sympathy and an admiration for the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King and for the gallantry that was displayed by this individual.
Harper and Mackenzie King, it might not be so well known, became extremely close friends. They spent many hours debating proper behaviour of men of the time, the gallantry, the gallant, I suppose. Harper retained this youthful enthusiasm, but King did not. Harper retained the ideals and idyllic dreams of youth. King became irritable about his friend's lack of ambition and his deeper and more reflective form of idealism that even at the turn of the century was commonly found in poets and perhaps a little less commonly in men of business and politics.
The memorial that was placed by King was a remembrance of Harper's gallantry and death in his attempt to rescue Miss Bessie Blair from drowning beneath the ice. It has also been called a farewell, not only to his friend but to the feeling that King probably lost some of the enthusiasm that Harper had, after he got into politics.
Incidentally it is not strictly true that Sir Galahad is the only monument to civil servants in Ottawa. Behind the National Library at the end of Wellington Street there is a handsome portrait statue of Sir Arthur Doughty,
Private Members' Business
Dominion Archivist, looking solemnly out over the river. He too was King's friend. Doughty's monument used to be in a more prominent position. I understand that it could have been in the front of the building, but rumour has it that a chief librarian who followed him had it moved to the back.
As to the substance of the motion of my hon. friend, I would like to bring to the attention of the House that the Department of Public Works, as well as adding to the statuary on the Hill, has been cleaning the Harper memorial and as far as possible restoring it to its original condition. It has been cleaned, the disastrous action of the road salt neutralized, and Galahad has been returned to very near his original state.
The member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is quite right in his observation that the site, even though it was moved a metre or two away from the immediate danger of the salt and heavy traffic, remains a potentially dangerous place for bronze and stone. The decision to leave him there was not, I can assure you, Madam Speaker, a slavish adherence to a principle of heritage restoration work or done without thought. Sir Galahad has been moved in the past and, generally speaking, is not bound too tightly to the notion that statues once placed should not be moved. In leaving the statue by the side of Wellington Street, the Department of Public Works acted in full consultation with conservators, the Federal Heritage Building Review Office and the National Capital Commission. A detailed analysis by a team of internationally recognized experts in the field of bronze conservation was made just after the Diefenbaker statue was erected.
Their recommendation was that Sir Galahad was well protected by the restoration process and by the layers of hard wax with which he is covered. He should be left there, not forever, but for the time being, until a number of issues important to the subject are addressed.
I want my hon. friend to listen to this because I think it is well thought out. Not too long ago, at the time of the debate on a previous motion by the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell calling for the erection of a statue of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, the former minister, Stewart Mclnnes, tabled a report to Parliament on commemorative statues of Canadian Prime Ministers and other eminent Canadians. In the course of the

November 21, 1991
Private Members' Business
deliberations surrounding the report the government recognized that the actual parliamentary precinct, the Hill itself, should really be reserved for statues and monuments of monarchs and parliamentarians, and notably Prime Ministers, notwithstanding that statues of others do exist on the Hill.
This is not a new idea. King had participated in the subcommittee work to find a place for this monument. He objected that it should be placed in an obscure and isolated part and fought with determination that it be located in a pre-eminent place on the Hill on the southeast lawn area. However, his colleagues at that time did not agree, not I think from any motive that would decline their respect for the civil service but because they were aware that the Hill precinct is a finite space and could easily be filled to capacity should free reign be given to unbridled political passion.
I do agree that in the matter of these historic monuments, monuments that will be seen, admired and studied by our great-grandchildren, we should avoid ad hoc actions that may be regretted later, however meritorious and well conceived the motion.
Almost every statue and monument presently on the Hill has been put there by a decision of the House of Commons that has had little bearing on any plan or clear thought for the effect of the object on the whole. It is, of course, the right of the House to make such decisions but perhaps not in the best interests of the future. Plans have been made in the past for the disposition of monuments on the Hill and all have been put aside in the heat of the sentiment that inevitably surrounds the proposal for the next statue or monument.
I would prefer to have such decisions made away from passion and part of an over-all plan such as that now being examined by the Board of Internal Economy. I hope my friend is aware that this has been taking place.
Another equally important consideration is the funding for all these works. I have to tell you that the Department of Public Works has been able to clean and restore these important monuments by using small amounts from the funds voted for the upkeep of the Parliament Buildings; from cash flow if you like. No
funds are available that are dedicated specifically to the upkeep of parliamentary monuments.
The result of that is that although, as you can see for yourself, about half of the 20 or so have been restored, the others will have to wait. For instance, it was our hope and the hope of Public Works officials that work could begin on the restoration of the National War Memorial in 1992. We all would have liked to see this jewel of a monument that means so much to all Canadians cleaned, repaired and pristine for the 125th anniversary of Confederation. But there simply is not sufficient money at this time and the project will have to be postponed for a little while. With such scarce funds it would be irresponsible to allow work to proceed without planning.
I can, however, assure members and the author of the motion in particular that the government recognizes the proposal is valid. The Department of Public Works will ensure that the matter is not put aside and that as funds become available, the relocation of Sir Galahad will be addressed in the proper context, that of an over-all plan.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to say a few words about the motion presented by my colleague, the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, as it relates to the Harper memorial statue and its relocation.
I listened very carefully to what the parliamentary secretary said in his intervention on behalf of the government and the belief that, yes, the motion of my friend and colleague is a good one and that when there is an opportunity and dollars available, he would be in favour of looking to move this particular statue to a better location.
We are not talking about a great deal of money here. For example, just this afternoon I was reading a clipping about how Treasury Board spent $250,000 to advertise how not to pay our civil servants because of the strike.
I am not fortunate enough to know exactly how much it would cost to have this particular statue moved, but I am sure the amount is quite small, probably a few thousand dollars maximum. Not too long ago in my own hometown we moved a statue. We got volunteers to put the statue on a vehicle and move it to another location. I do not want to be partisan but I would say to the
November 21, 1991

government opposite that the argument really has no merit in this discussion.
Therefore, it would become a matter of where the statue should go. Obviously my colleague is suggesting its present location is not a good one and that it should be moved. He is suggesting that it be moved on to Parliament Hill where it would be somewhat safer. I believe that is a legitimate argument. It obviously needs clarification as to exactly where it should be placed.
I have to agree with the member opposite that statutes cannot just be put here, there and everywhere. Knowing how sophisticated and somewhat arrogant members of Parliament are sometimes, we would all want our statue left behind when we leave. It is not bad enough that we have to take our chairs with us, we would probably want to leave a statue behind as well.
I am very interested in the part of the member's motion which suggests that we dedicate this statute to the employees of the federal government for their valuable contribution to Canada.
As a labour critic and a member who is very much involved in what the workers in this place do, I think that is a very legitimate area of concern of my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
In looking around at this place and the different statues there are on the Hill, there does not seem to be enough discussion or enough reflection of the merits of that particular quote I just read from the motion. Maybe we too often take for granted the importance of the people who keep this place running and the importance of the civil servants across Canada who put in the extra hours it takes to make this country the great country it is.
I strongly urge the government to reconsider the fact that on the one hand it feels that this motion has merit and on the other hand it is not prepared to accept the motion and set up a committee and go through the process of moving this particular statue, putting it in its proper place. At the same time, it should also consider using it to pay homage to those individuals who have worked all their lives for their country as civil servants and those who are still employed by the Government of Canada.
I think we should go that one little step, especially in consideration of the difficulties we have been having with the public servants and the strikes and the back-to-
Private Members' Business
work legislation we were involved in that was debated very strongly in this place.
That would go a long way to show our civil servants, the people who are working for the public day in and day out, that we care that much about them to make it a little bit of a prestigious memorial by putting a plaque on a statute commemorating their activities.
In conclusion, I wish to say I support this motion whole-heartedly. It shows that we in this place are not just thinking of ourselves as a lot of Canadians think we do. In essence, we are thinking of our public servants and we are also thinking of the past which is something that we have to be very vigilant to remember.
The past is what has got us to the point we are at today. As soon as we forget about our past, it becomes an anarchy in this country. Having said that, I would hope that the government will be prepared to accept this motion in its entirety and get on with the job.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate today on the motion of the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell which has been added to by my colleagues on both sides of the House.
It is very fitting in a way that this motion, with the intent that it has, should arise from that particular member and colleague in the House who, as he intimated himself a few moments ago, has had the unusual and unique experience of having started work on the Hill after he left school and then moving on to become a member of the House of Commons. I am not surprised that he, of all of us, should be the one to bring forward this particular suggestion.
I also agree with him that we are not dealing with a partisan subject. However, that some of us on the government side may not feel it appropriate to pursue and support his motion is not an indication of political partisanship.
It is not my intention today to debate the merits of moving the Harper memorial statue from its present site on Wellington Street to a site on the grounds of Parliament Hill. The reasons are straightforward. They are not emotional reasons at all but rather reasons that are based more on criteria that do not exist and would allow for that at the present time.

Private Members' Business
Indeed, the regulations that govern the placement of commemorations on the grounds of Parliament Hill are very clear in this regard. They state that only Prime Ministers and monarch? be considered for this honour. I notice the hon. member shaking his head. Maybe there is room for debate there but my information is that Parliament Hill is reserved for monarchs and former Prime Ministers.
Henry Albert Harper's life is worthy of further consideration. The hon. member for Glengariy-Prescott- Russell has touched on some of it. I would like to elaborate more on that because he did see a variety of achievements in his life.
I do not believe that those achievements in themselves, those contributions, were national in their significance and therefore worthy of his statue being placed on the Hill with former Prime Ministers and former monarchs.
In fact, were the siting of a commemoration to Henry Harper to be considered today, it certainly would not qualify for the high profile site it currently occupies.
In other words, people who are recognized for such deeds of bravery are not recognized in that fashion today, although I am not attempting to take away from the fact that he was appropriately honoured in those days.
To support our position, I would like to sketch briefly the life that Henry Harper led before his untimely death 90 years ago.
When he arrived in Ottawa in 1900 to become deputy minister of the newly formed Department of Labour, William Lyon Mackenzie King encountered a number of friends from his undergraduate years at the University of Toronto. Among them was Henry Harper, a young man from Cookstown, Ontario.
While Mr. King had furthered his studies in Toronto and the United States after graduating in 1895, Harper had pursued a career in journalism. The two men rekindled their friendship when they met in Ottawa five years later.
By 1900, acting as both parliamentary correspondent and city editor for a Montreal newspaper, Mr. Harper was a natural choice for King as his assistant editor on the department's new publication The Labour Gazette.
Both King and Harper were deeply affected by the condition of the working poor in the industrial society. They sought in their new roles to be knights of the 20th century, so to speak: gallant, chivalrous and dedicated to the selfless service of others and their own political ambitions. Harper in fact had even placed in his room a reproduction of his favourite painting Sir Galahad.
During the winter months, both King and Harper devoted much of their time to prolonged reading and intense debates on the subject of chivalry. One of their favourite authors was Alfred Lord Tennyson, whose epic poem about the medieval King Arthur and his knights, entitled Idylls of the King, played a special role in providing them with an ideal of manly conduct.
Winter also meant outdoor sports. Skating parties were especially popular, including those organized by the Governor General and his wife, Lord and Lady Minto. Speaking of skating parties and tragedy, I recall my mother telling me years ago that she was skating here in Ottawa at the skating rink when the Parliament Buildings burned down in 1916.1 could not help but recall that event when I touch now on what happened on this particular night.
Among those invited to this skating party by the Governor General were young debutantes like Bessie Blair, who has been referred to previously, one of the daughters of Andrew G. Blair, a senior member of the cabinet in the Liberal government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
On Friday, December 5, 1901, while acting as Deputy Minister during one of King's absences from the city, Harper went out to skate on the Ottawa River. On his way home he apparently met and joined a group of young people coming from one of the Minto skating parties near Rideau Hall. Moments later, however, the ice gave way and Harper saw two of the group fall through the ice into the freezing water.
While one young man reached safety, Bessie Blair was clearly in great difficulty and drowning. Despite pleas from others not to risk his life, Harper dived in to save her.
Their bodies were not recovered until the following morning.
Within three days of the drowning, and on what would have been Harper's 28th birthday, a large group of citizens, as was mentioned earlier, met in Ottawa City
November 21, 1991

Hall to express their desire to commemorate Harper's gallantry.
King served on the committee appointed to oversee the project and played a very active role. He proposed, for example, that the memorial should derive its inspiration from Harper's favourite painting of Sir Galahad.
King was equally active on the subcommittee appointed to select a site, which is being discussed so avidly today. Resisting suggestions to place the monument in an isolated park, he fought vigorously for a central location and preferred one on Parliament Hill in the southeast corner of the grounds. The government refused King's reports.
Although his endeavours failed, King did succeed in placing it close by: exactly on the north side of Wellington Street at the head of Metcalfe, at the main ceremonial approach to Parliament from the south.
We recognize Henry Harper's accomplishments, both as a reporter and during his brief tenure as a civil servant. We also acknowledge his bravery that winter day in 1901 when he died attempting to save the life of Ms. Blair.
We respect Henry Harper's actions, indeed his sacrifice. That is why a commemoration of Mr. Harper now stands at the gateway to Parliament Hill commanding a prestigious location in our capital.
An illustration in that respect is clear in the 1990 decision to remove the Sir Galahad statue for restorative work required following the long-term exposure to pollutants, as my colleague alluded to previously. A joint NCC and Public Works Canada committee subsequently decided that the statue should be replaced close to its previous location and this was done late in 1990.
I would like to remind the members however that in April 1988 a report commissioned by the National Capital Commission entitled "Capital Commemoration" recommended, and I emphasize this, that only commemorations of former Prime Ministers be placed on Parliament Hill. A program to erect statues of all deceased former Prime Ministers on Parliament Hill was approved by cabinet in September and cabinet approved Parliament Hill as the location for future statues until space no longer permits. Since there are six deceased Prime
Adjournment Debate
Ministers who have not yet been commemorated in addition to the statue of Queen Elizabeth to be unveiled next year, space is at a premium.
It was for those reasons that the siting of Sir Galahad on Parliament Hill was not an issue when the subject was discussed last year.
Given the memorial's current high profile, the restorative work that has been carried out, and cabinet's approval of the NCC's commemoration's policy, we do not believe that the Harper memorial should be relocated to the grounds of Parliament Hill.
I thank you for the opportunity to offer my comments on this subject.

Marie at Algoma Steel and in Elliot Lake at the operating uranium mines there. In fact, some 2,400 workers were laid off in Elliot Lake mines last year. They

I was advised in late August that 260 of these workers were eligible for the program for older worker adjustment. It provides something like 70 per cent of the benefit that they would receive under unemployment insurance as an older worker pension from age 55 to age 64 when they become eligible for the Old Age Security pension, Canada Pension and other pensions.
The minister responded at that time, indicating that the Government of Canada, his office and his department had approved the application for these 260 workers and that the matter still had to be dealt with by the Treasury Board.

If the minister is able to respond in a positive way and if the Ontario government has agreed to this program for some 260 workers, about 200 from the Rio Algom Mines, the two that shut down a year ago, and 60 from Denison Mines Limited, the government will be able to move rapidly to interview these individual workers to assess their needs and to be able to provide the full benefits of the Program for Older Worker Adjustment.

out. I am very pleased that the government here has approved it. Madam Speaker, I too rise today in order to get some answers to a particular question that I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration on June 18, 1991.
I asked about the fact that we are looking at some sort of national retraining strategy and programs to be implemented in this country because of the restructuring that is going on due to the free trade agreement.
People in this country will know that we are in a recession and that there are some difficult times when there is over 10 per cent unemployment. There are over one million Canadians on unemployment insurance and, in essence, during the election of 1988, the first election that I ran in, we on this side of the House at least asked the government if when we put this new regime called free trade into place there be worker adjustment programs put in place in order to deal with those who would be considered to be losers under this new agreement between the United States and Canada.
During Question Period on June 18, 1991 I asked the minister if he could explain to us in detail what took place with respect to the 10,800 displaced workers in the auto industry and the 9,200 displaced workers in the steel industry. I would like to say to the members opposite and to the minister's parliamentary secretary in this adjournment debate that it frustrates me to no end and all Canadians, when you ask very serious questions concerning the steel industry which is in big, big trouble, and the auto parts industry which is big, big trouble with a lot of those employees.
We are not naive in this place, and neither are Canadian workers. We understand that in a global market there are going to be changes that need to be looked at. In essence what I am trying to say is when we ask that question I do not want to get the answer I got from the minister which was: "That side of the House does not understand the issue and therefore come and talk to me after Question Period and I will tell you just why it is that you do not understand".
We understand very well that we are in big trouble. The Chamber of Commerce has come out and said so, as we have said for many, many months now. The restructuring going on in our economy is going to cause severe problems for a long period of time. We need those adjustment programs and we need them now. We want them now. We want an explanation as to what effect they will have in the different sectors.
In a community like mine in which forestry is the number one employer, we would like to know if there was a downturn in that particular sector what the game plan of the government would be. I am hoping in the few

minutes that the parliamentary secretary has he will just give us a snapshot of what this government is doing in order that we can tell our constituents and all employees who are frightened because of what is going on out there that there is hope and we are planning for the future and we are looking ahead to help them with their problems.

speechtext:
: Madam Speaker, I would like to respond in greater detail to the questions placed by my hon. friend, the member from Kenora- Rainy River on July 18 on the free trade agreement.
At this stage it is really too early to come to any definite conclusions about the impact of the free trade agreement. There are encouraging signs however. Trade and investment have shown positive trends in the last three years. Exports of end products to the United States increased $4 billion between 1988 and 1990. Between
1989	and 1990 manufacturing investment in Canada rose 15 per cent. Canada's 16 per cent gain in investment and new plant and equipment was second-and I would underline this-only to Japan among the G-7 nations. In
1990	there was a net inflow of foreign investment from all countries of $4.3 billion into Canada, the first net inflow in more than 15 years.
The dispute settlement mechanisms of the free trade agreement are working very well. The free trade agreement has led to a reduced number of trade disputes and the dispute settlement mechanism and procedures which have been established will help to deal with future trade disputes as they arise.
Job losses over the past year should not be attributed to the free trade agreement. It is only one of the several factors including wage rates, business cycles and the value of the Canadian dollar which influence employment patterns in Canada. While there have been positive developments, some workers may still be adversely affected by structural adjustments taking place within the Canadian economy. These individuals can and are assisted through a wide range of general labour market programs which the Department of Employment and Immigration Canada has in place.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question posed to the minister regarding the value of the Canadian dollar has been in front of the House for many days. Unfortunately some of the industries involved in exports seem to think that lowering the Canadian dollar will solve all their export problems. If we do that we will create a lot of import problems and we could create further problems for the debt we have at the present time, much of which is offshore.
There are great pressures on the Canadian dollar. The Bank of Canada can balance some of them in the short term. However, in the long term you cannot do anything more than allow the free market to work. That is what is happening today. Today, the Canadian dollar is at about 88 cents, down a little bit.
Look at the pressures on the dollar. Municipalities across the country, large municipalities, borrow offshore. Provinces borrow offshore. Large corporations which say that our bank rates are too high issue treasury bills on their own or borrow money offshore. That places pressure on the Canadian dollar. For years the Government of Canada encouraged provinces and municipalities to borrow offshore rather than place extra demands on the very limited investment capital in this country that results from our small population.
We feel that the dollar is going to come down. However I have to say quite honestly that if I were running a business today, which I am not, I would not base the success of my business on the level of the Canadian dollar. That is not a good way to do business. In the short run we could perhaps cause an order here or there. However, in the longer run we are better to work
Adjournment Debate
to keep inflation down, keep interest rates down and improve productivity in this country. That is a much better way to go about it than to impose a fixed rate of exchange on the Canadian dollar, for example.
The hon. member is a certified general accountant, or at least I believe he is. He knows the financial situation quite well and is very familiar with it. I can understand him wishing to speak on behalf of his constituents in the paper industry. The paper industry is under a lot of difficulty today and we can see some bright spots down the lane for it. However, we do not think that the solution is to fix the Canadian dollar at a lower rate.

Madam Speaker, on October 11, 1991 I asked the Secretary of State a question about Canada's educational situation concerning government funding. At the time the minister said that on a per capita basis we spend as much or more than any other country. Then the House leader stepped in and said that as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product Canada is second only to Sweden. The Secretary of State replied by saying: "absolutely".
The fact that he mentioned we were second to Sweden triggered a need for a little research in my mind. I have the report published this year by the National Science and Engineering Research Council of Canada. In it there is a graph comparing Canada to seven countries around the world. The report starts by stating that: "International comparisons show that Canada's spending", on research and development only, "is one of the lowest of major industrialized countries". In fact, it does compare spending as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product. It goes as follows: Sweden, 2.93 per cent; United States, 2.83 per cent; Japan, 2.78 per cent; Germany, 2.71 per cent; United Kingdom, 2.42 per cent; France, 2.33 per cent; and Canada, 1.38 per cent.
As you can see, Madam Speaker, statistics which were published and accepted by the Government of Canada show that Canada is nowhere to be seen when it comes to spending on educational elements such as research and development.
The government's record of last year alone shows there has been a cut of $485 million for education in its latest budget. The contributions to training have

dropped by 4.6 per cent this year in spite of an over-all increase in government spending of 4.3 per cent.
As a matter of fact, between 1986 and 1994, the government eliminated $9.5 billion in transfer payments to the provinces. According to the latest statistics, by the year 2004 absolutely no federal funds will be going toward education and to the provinces in transfer payments.
While federal funding for education has been decreasing, student costs have been on the rise. Looking at post-secondary education, for example, Statistics Canada reports that Ontario tuition fees alone have increased by 53 per cent since 1983-84.
Likewise the cost of living has increased. On top of the cost of living, the federal government has introduced a 3 per cent tax on student loans and has applied the GST to books. This has added hundreds of dollars to many students' financial burdens and hit hardest those least able to afford to pay for their education.
I am here to ask the government: Would you please, members of the government, clarify to the Canadian public how you can say on one hand that we are on the leading edge when it comes to spending on research and development and, on the other hand, we have a tremendous number of cuts in areas such as education and transfer payments?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know the hon. member for Ottawa Centre is concerned about education and I wish to assure him that I am too, because before I was elected to Parliament I was a teacher.
Contrary to what the hon. member suggests, Canada plays a leading role because it is clearly determined to promote excellence in education while respecting provincial jurisdiction. As the Secretary of State said, we devote a larger percentage of our GNP to education than most countries do. Canada comes second for the proportion of young people registered in post-secondary educational institutions, right after the United States.
To help us remain in the forefront of human resource development, the government recently announced the prosperity initiative, of which education is a key element.
Regarding the last part of the hon. member's question, I would like to say that the government has not cut funding for post-secondary education. We froze spending in order to control the national debt and we are proud of our success in this field. Moreover, although we had to limit transfer payments to the provinces to do so, the total funding available for post-secondary education continues to increase.
Thus assistance for post-secondary education under Established Programs Financing rose by $80 million in 1990-91 and $70 million in 1991-92, to reach nearly $6 billion this year. Of this total, about $2 billion is in cash. Total transfers are to increase to reflect population growth in future years.
In conclusion, in addition to providing financial aid to the provinces and territories the federal government is increasing its direct support for higher education through programs like funding for the University Research Council and the Canadian Student Aid Program. In all, it is estimated that about $2 billion will be given in direct support in 1991-92.

Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to pursue some questions I had asked of the government regarding the completion of the signing of a very important forest agreement between the Government of Canada and the province of Nova Scotia. In fact, back on March 26 of this year I asked the forestry committee of the Minister of Forestry when that agreement would be finally signed. The minister said at that time that he had a good fix on the Nova Scotia situation; the funds had been identified and he did not anticipate a delay.
Later in the year on October 28 in the House I asked the minister when he would be able to sign this important agreement. He answered on that date that he would be able to sign the new agreement as soon as a date could be arranged.

Our staff has consulted and checked with the Government of Nova Scotia and as of Thesday, in any case, there has been no indication from the Government of Canada as to when the minister would actually sign this particular agreement. It is very important that he does.
I hope when the member responding from the government side comments on the importance of this agreement, he can give the commitment that the minister gave some nine months ago that an agreement would be signed at any time. I hope the member responding can tell us when the minister is going to sign the new forest agreement with Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be given this opportunity to address this House on our achievements in the area of sustainable forestry in Nova Scotia.
As you may know, the agreement was negotiated in two phases in Nova Scotia. The first phase saw the signing of a two-year, 1989-1991, interim agreement, the Canada-Nova Scotia cooperation agreement for forestry development, 1989-1991, CAFD I. This interim agreement had a major impact in two very important areas. First, it was instrumental in building upon the momentum established through previous forestry agreements. Second, it represented a new beginning toward more integrated and sustainable forestry development.
Twenty-four million federal dollars, 55 per cent of total $45 million agreement was invested in the Nova Scotia forest sector in key areas of forest management, applied research, development and technology transfer, and communications and education.
The two years saw us maintain annual silviculture targets needed to sustain a healthy and diversified forest
